104-inaugural-address-of-franklin-delano:
America in March 1933 faced bank failures, unemployment, and fear itself. Franklin Delano Roosevelt's first inaugural address, given March 4, 1933, opens with a promise of candor and decision. He declares that the only thing to fear is fear itself.

Roosevelt blames money changers and failed leadership, then pledges action on banks, farms, and jobs. He asks Congress for broad power to fight the emergency, as if against a foreign foe. The speech rallied a frightened nation behind the New Deal. Its opening line became an American motto. Roosevelt's pledge of action shaped the Hundred Days that followed his inauguration.
1198-robbery-under-arms-a-story-of-life-:
Rolf Boldrewood was the pen name of Thomas Alexander Browne. He tells of Dick Marston, a young Australian who drifts into bushranging with Captain Starlight's gang. Dick lives by horse theft, hold-ups, and narrow escapes, and he narrates his own fall and his long road back toward honesty.

The tale moves through goldfields, stations, and wild bush, with chases, trials, and a love that waits for Dick's reform. Boldrewood, who knew the bush as a police magistrate, writes its life with firsthand color. The novel became Australia's classic bushranger tale, and it still rides well.
12421-practical-exercises-in-english:
Huber Gray Buehler's 1895 exercises, made for use with Hill's Foundations of Rhetoric at the Hotchkiss School, teach English by practice. Chapters cover good use, articles, nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives and adverbs, prepositions and conjunctions, with appendix and index.

The opening chapter asks why one word serves better than another in composition, testing passages from the King James Bible for present use. Students work through set sentences, correcting and choosing, rather than memorising rules alone. The book shows late nineteenth-century school rhetoric at work: careful, graded and aimed at clear, correct writing.
12478-books-and-characters-french-englis:
Lytton Strachey's 1922 papers, Books and Characters, French and English, reprint essays from the Independent Review, the New Quarterly, the Athenaeum and the Edinburgh Review. Contents run from Racine, Sir Thomas Browne and Shakespeare's final period to Madame du Deffand, Voltaire in England, Rousseau, Blake and Lady Hester Stanhope.

A dialogue, printed here for the first time from a manuscript said to be in Voltaire's hand, joins studies of Voltaire's tragedies, his quarrel with Frederick the Great and the Rousseau affair. Strachey writes with wit, irony and sharp portraiture, judging writers by character as much as by work. The book shows the Strachey manner at its most polished, learned and mischievous.
13597-a-tale-of-a-lonely-parish:
F. Marion Crawford's 1886 tale of a lonely parish was dedicated to his mother from Sorrento on Christmas Day 1885. It opens with the Reverend Augustin Ambrose, growing old, sight troubling him, weary of Thucydides, Homer, Todhunter's conic sections, and even beloved Horace. Pupils sent because they cannot keep up, or because schooling left them unready for university, tire him further.

Skating in the afternoon brings the squire, Mrs. Goddard, Nellie, and John to a pond black as a hat and firm enough to bear an ox. A vicar hesitates over telling Gall, an old chatterbox, a truth that talking always brings out. Crawford writes a quiet English parish novel of clergy, pupils, neighbours, and the small moral choices of country life.
14800-the-present-state-of-wit-1711-and-:
John Gay's The Present State of Wit, first published in 1711, appears here in an Augustan Reprint Society edition with an introduction by Donald F. Bond. Gay surveys wit in Queen Anne's London, judging writers, coffeehouse talk and the fashions of polite letters.

Excerpts from The English Theophrastus, or the Manners of the Age, from 1702, with an introduction by W. Earl Britton, add a second view of manners and character. The society's series, priced at seventy-five cents and issued six times a year to members, aimed to put scarce Augustan texts back in students' hands. Together the pieces show wit as social currency in early Georgian England.
15656-representation-of-the-impiety-and-:
This Augustan Reprint Society pamphlet, series three, number two, reprints two anonymous 1704 attacks on the English stage, with an introduction by Emmett L. Avery and a bibliographical note. The society published it in March 1947, at seventy-five cents, with general editors from Michigan and California. Members paid two dollars fifty a year for six publications.

The first tract represents the impiety and immorality of the English stage. The second offers some thoughts concerning the stage. Together they show the early eighteenth-century moral campaign against the theatre, when critics charged plays with corrupting manners and faith. Avery's introduction and notes set the pamphlets in their moment. The reprint lets modern readers hear the anti-stage case in its own fierce, period voice.
16288-oddsfish:
Oddsfish opens in a royal chamber where the King, interrupted by a visitor, cries that he is being preached to and sends the intruder away. The King had sent for Mr. Mallock to reprimand him severely, yet finds Mallock holding the whip instead, and jokes that little Ken is nothing to it: Mallock should have been a bishop. Laughter gives way to gravity as the King insists on his reprimand, though Mallock will escape the guard-room this time.

A sundial, the King notes, is not so important as a Christian lady, and a bunch of raisins is not legally a blow in the face. From such witty, dangerous talk grows a historical romance of Charles the Second's court, with priests, plots, and conscience. Readers who like Restoration intrigue will enjoy its sparkling, perilous world.
16362-the-glugs-of-gosh:
C. J. Dennis spins a comic verse tale of the Glugs, a foolish folk in the city of Gosh, in this 1917 book with pictures by Hal Gye. The quest opens the story, then Joi the Glug, his son Sym, the Swanks, a seer, a debate, and a little red dog all take their turns. An old Gosh rhyme tells how to meet a Glug: pluck hairs from a rug, blow two away, burn one, and swallow the rest.

The verse is playful and satirical, poking fun at pomp, schools, and wise men who know little. Dennis writes for readers who enjoy nonsense with a sting. The Glugs' silly wisdom still reads as a light, funny fable of human folly.
16573-the-honorable-senator-sage-brush:
Francis Lynde's 1913 novel follows a western senator through bosses, highbinders, and a battle royal over railroads and power. Chapters run from Because Patricia Said No through The Boss, At Wartrace Hall, The Queen's Gambit, and The Great Game to a cry in the night and field headquarters. The frontispiece catches a vice-president snapping over a retainer.

Lynde, who knew western railroading at first hand, writes with inside detail on lobbies, deals, and desert politics. The tale mixes romance with a sharp look at how the West was governed. Readers of political adventure will find it brisk, knowing, and full of local color.
17499-a-jolly-by-josh:
Josh, writing as Uncle Josh, privately printed this jolly in 1902, in the form of letters to Charlie. The book opens on a Lake Shore Limited train crossing the continent, where the writer, with a spare moment in the rear car, studies his fellow travellers and finds them uniformly uninteresting. His mind wanders out of the window instead, and a story grows from the ride.

Later letters close with a gift: a cheque to buy a pony, since at the writer's age a trip through the Rocky Mountains had awakened his love of riding. Readers get a light, epistolary jaunt, humorous and personal. The book suits readers of railway humour and of private-press curiosities.
17594-lectures-on-language-as-particular:
William S. Balch delivered these lectures on language before the Young People's Institute of Providence, and published them there in 1838 with B. Cranston and Company. The full title promises lectures on language as particularly connected with English grammar, designed for teachers and advanced learners. Balch takes Pythagoras as his motto: silence is better than unmeaning words.

Institute members thanked Balch for lectures they called highly entertaining and greatly instructive, and praised his plain, rational principles for explaining English grammar. They had long wanted a system a child or adult could grasp. Readers get an early American work on the philosophy of language, earnest, systematic, and meant for the classroom.
17613-the-land-of-the-black-mountain-the:
Reginald Wyon and Gerald Prance wrote this account of two Englishmen in Montenegro. It was first published in March 1903 and issued in a new and cheaper edition in 1905 by Methuen in London, with fifty-one pictures. The authors dedicate the book, by kind permission, to Prince Nicolas of Montenegro. Its opening chapter surveys Montenegro's position, people, and character.

Montenegrins appear as honest, patriotic, and fond of arms, likened to Homeric Greeks, with chapters on women, manners, costume, religion, and hatred of Austria. History runs from Roman conquest in 300 before the common era to the present prince. Readers get an Edwardian travel book, affectionate toward a small mountain state.
17647-the-strange-case-of-cavendish:
Randall Parrish, author of The Devil's Own and When Wilderness Was King, wrote this mystery novel, published by A. L. Burt Company in New York by arrangement with George H. Doran Company, copyright 1918. Chapters open with the reaching of a decision, the body on the floor, and Mr. Enright declaring himself. A breath of suspicion and the track of a crime follow.

At Steinway's, Miss Donovan arrives, a gang of enemies gathers, and a night and a morning pass, with a new angle ahead. Readers get a popular mystery of murder, pursuit, and revelation, in Parrish's sturdy style. The book suits readers of early twentieth-century detective fiction.
17806-foes-in-ambush:
Captain Charles King wrote Foes in Ambush in 1893, a soldier's tale of Arizona in the Apache wars, printed in Philadelphia by Lippincott. King served in the United States Army, and his tales drew on his own years on the frontier.

The book opens at sunset in the desert, where a paymaster guards his safe in a corral near the Santa Maria pass. Apaches haunt the heat, the march must be made by night, and ambush waits on the trail. King writes with a soldier's eye for drill, dust, and danger. It is a brisk, old-style army romance, with the era's harsh views of Native foes plain on the page.
18070-poets-and-dreamers-studies-and-tra:
Lady Gregory wrote Poets and Dreamers in 1903, printed in Dublin and New York, as studies and translations from the Irish. Gregory, a founder of the Irish literary revival, dedicates the book to undergraduates of Trinity College, urging them to find the best in folks nearest home.

Chapters cover Raftery the blind poet, west Irish ballads, Jacobite songs, Douglas Hyde's poems, Boer ballads in Ireland, mountain faith, herb-healing, and workhouse dreams. Gregory writes with love for Irish speech and folk. The book is a warm, key text of the revival, and a fine door into Irish verse and lore.
18400-isopel-berners-the-history-of-cert:
George Borrow's Isopel Berners tells the history of certain doings in a Staffordshire dingle in July 1825, as an episode in Borrow's autobiography. Thomas Seccombe edited the text with introduction and notes for Hodder and Stoughton in 1901. Borrow, author of The Romany Rye, was born in East Dereham, Norfolk, where people, he says, eat the best dumplings and speak the purest English.

The episode opens in May 1825, when Borrow, known among gypsies as the word-master, leaves London on foot and by coach for Amesbury and Salisbury, then strikes north. In a small beer-house he meets a tinker and his wife, the tinker downcast after a rival, Bosville the flaming tinman, intimidated him. Readers get Borrow at his most vivid: road, dingle, gypsy talk, and a summer that becomes legend.
18511-historic-tales-the-romance-of-real:
Charles Morris wrote this fourth volume of his Historical Tales in 1893, covering English history in story form. Its short tales run from the coming of Christianity to England and King Alfred's fight with the Danes, through Robin Hood, Wallace at Stirling, and Bruce at Bannockburn. Later pieces cover the Field of the Cloth of Gold, Cromwell, the flight of Prince Charles, and Nelson at Trafalgar.

Morris retells each event as a vivid scene, with heroes, sieges, and escapes at the fore. The book closes with Queen Victoria's jubilees, bringing the tale near his own day. It works well as a first, story-led path into English history.
18542-how-to-cook-fish:
Olive Green wrote this fish cookery book as a working manual for the kitchen, built on catching, seasoning, and serving fish in many forms. Its contents run from catching unshelled fish and fish in season to court bouillons and a hundred simple fish sauces.

The bulk of the book gives numbered ways to cook each kind of fish, from bass and cod to halibut, herring, and salmon. A cook who wants one kind of fish done many ways will find dozens of plain, clear directions here, laid out by species rather than by course.
19457-historic-tales-the-romance-of-real:
Charles Morris wrote this seventh volume of his Historic Tales, on Spain, published in London in the late eighteen hundreds. It retells the deeds behind Spanish legend: King Wamba, the battle of Guadalete, the Cid Campeador, the cave of Covadonga, and the long war for Granada.

Later tales follow Peter the Cruel, whose murdered kin were avenged by Henry, and the Great Captain of the Granada campaigns. Morris calls his series the romance of reality, and the volume shows history told as story, with heroes, stratagems, and rival kings in quick succession.
19537-punky-dunk-and-the-gold-fish:
This little picture story tells in verse of Punky Dunk, a fat black and white cat of tender years, and his curiosity about a goldfish globe. He sleeps in a straw box with his nose on his paw, peeps at a caged bird, and longs to see how fishes drink.

At last he bounds to the stand, sets his paws on the rim, and bends his head down with tongue out, to the fishes' alarm. Told and drawn for a good little child, the book is a gentle joke on kitten curiosity and the trouble it invites.
19704-a-pocket-dictionary-welsh-english:
W. Richards compiled this pocket dictionary of Welsh and English, printed at Wrexham in the mid eighteen hundreds and sold in London. Its Welsh preface notes a hopeful sign: more Welsh people learning English, and more English summer visitors trying to learn Welsh.

Entries run from surnames and over-shots to conquest, leases, and laying open, each with part of speech and plain sense. The little book served travelers, learners, and neighbors on both sides of the language border. Richards made the book pocket-sized, so travelers could carry it on summer roads. Sample entries run from Diewyllys for intestate to Difalch for void of pride, in tight pocket form.
19851-more-tish:
Mary Roberts Rinehart created Tish, the formidable spinster adventurer, in popular stories. More Tish, dated 1921, continues her escapades. Tish's friends narrate, often in dismay at her schemes. One recalls reading aloud to Tish during an attack of neuralgia. All that while, Tish was scheming and planning in silence. She never said a word of her plan. Her friends learned to expect the worst.

Letitia Carberry, called Tish, drives cars, solves problems, and defies convention. Rinehart mixes comedy with genuine suspense around her. The stories ran in magazines to wide delight. Tish became a byword for the unstoppable older woman. More Tish gathers that fun in book form. It is light fiction with real snap.
2084-the-way-of-all-flesh:
Samuel Butler began this novel about 1872 and worked on it until 1884, but he held it back, dissatisfied, and it appeared only after his death in 1902. It follows Ernest Pontifex through a rigid family, school, and church. Butler's friends published the novel in 1903, a year after his death, as he had wished.

Butler uses Ernest's life to test his ideas on heredity and habit, showing how parents, clergy, and custom shape a son. The novel is frank, funny, and critical, and it stands as a classic Victorian attack on pious respectability. Ernest's escape from family and church mirrors Butler's own break with Victorian piety.
22247-if-you-touch-them-they-vanish:
Gouverneur Morris published If You Touch Them They Vanish in 1913, a novel of wealth and its discontents. Old Martha, the housekeeper, wonders if the Poor Boy will have a smile for her. He had so many smiles in the baby days, the growing-up days, and the college days. She remembers the Christmas he wrapped a grand fur coat round her shoulders and kissed her cheek.

The Poor Boy is rich in money and poor in everything that matters. Morris sends him searching for a life that vanishes when grasped, as the title warns. The book is a fable of American money written by a great-grandson of a Founding Father. Its sentiment once made it a beloved gift book.
22324-pushed-and-the-return-push:
Pushed and the Return Push tells of service in the First World War. No author is named in the catalog record. The narrator reaches Brigade Headquarters by makeshift means after a German retreat.

A lorry lift from railhead covers the first stretch of the trip. Then a horse borrowed from the Divisional Ammunition Column does the rest. The village found at the end had been held by the Germans. They left it in their spring 1917 retreat. Details like these ground the account in daily army life. Readers get war as transport, mud, and borrowed horses, not only as battle.
22665-christian-gellert-s-last-christmas:
Berthold Auerbach wrote Christian Gellert's Last Christmas, a tale from German Tales as published for American readers. The catalog record gives no year. Auerbach, famed for village stories of the Black Forest, here honors Christian Fürchtegott Gellert, the beloved Leipzig professor and fable writer of the eighteenth century.

The sample praises Gellert's teaching: his lessons were for life, and his life itself was a lesson. Many victories over trouble and temptation, the narrator says, began in that lecture hall at Gellert's feet. Around such reverence the story builds its Christmas close, as the old teacher's strength fails. Auerbach's tale is less plot than portrait, a tribute to a teacher whose goodness outlived him. It preserves the moral warmth German readers cherished in both men.
22846-the-ground-ash:
Two cottage children charm the narrator of The Ground Ash, a sketch by Mary Russell Mitford. At each sentence Bessy dips a small curtsy. Harry, hatless, touches the forelock of hair instead, in his own version of respect. Yet both children stay perfectly frank and unfearing, civil and respectful without stiffness.

Mitford lingers on their industry, content, and helpfulness, qualities she found delightful to watch and to think about. The ground ash of the title, a young tree, belongs to the same world of small rural goods. Little happens beyond a visit and talk. The pleasure lies in the people. Like her best sketches, this one preserves the manners of English cottage life as she saw them, in fine detail.
23033-classic-french-course-in-english:
William Cleaver Wilkinson defends his plan in Classic French Course in English. No school tradition, Wilkinson admits, can choose his route for him. French writing is no thinned ruin. It lives whole, with no great member yet torn away by time. The teacher must choose, and answer for the choice.

Wilkinson's answer is a guided tour of French classics for English readers, in translation and summary. Great names from Rabelais forward get their chapters, with extracts to taste the originals' flavor. The course aimed to give busy adults a real map of a foreign literature. Its judgments are confident Victorian ones. Readers can still use the map, checking its roads against their own reading as they go.
23680-sex-avoided-subjects-discussed-in-:
Henry Stanton published this frank advice book in 1922, promising to discuss in plain English subjects most books of the day avoided. He argues that the happiness of men and women depends largely on a rational understanding of sex, which cannot be ignored even though animals treat it as a simple instinct.

Ten chapters carry the reader from the cell to the human being. They move through childhood and adolescence in boys and girls, into marriage for husband and wife, and on to sex diseases and the bond between love and sex. Stanton writes as an educator, not a scold: climate, work, wealth, and morals all shape human sexual life, and knowledge, he insists, serves readers better than silence.
23764-the-bramble-bush:
Randall Garrett published The Bramble Bush in Analog in August 1962. Its title comes from the nursery rhyme of the man who jumped into a bramble bush and scratched out both his eyes. Its hero is Peter de Hooch, who wakes dreaming that the moon has blown up, to the sound of a great cr-r-r-ump.

The room is dark except for a glowing night-light, and Peter pads barefoot to the switch under light lunar gravity. Nothing seems out of place, yet something woke him. Garrett builds a lunar mystery from that small disturbance, in the manner of a man who knows he should not go back into trouble, and goes anyway.
24121-as-long-as-you-wish:
John O'Keefe wrote this science fiction tale for Astounding Science Fiction in June 1955. A patient named Charles J. Fisher, once a professor of philosophy at Reiser College, comes to a doctor with a coin he had made as a student. Each side reads that the statement on the other side is false, so reading it traps the reader in a loop.

Fisher links the coin to a sphere dug from an earth fault after a quake near Manila, and to a circular system of time in which events retrace themselves without end. O'Keefe builds the puzzle from talk and clues rather than action. Readers get a short, brain-teasing story about paradox, time, and a mind caught in its own circle.
24382-vigorish:
Walter Bupp wrote this science fiction story, with pictures by Petrizzo, for Astounding Science Fiction in June 1960. Its blurb asks a question: if it takes a thief to catch a thief, what does it take to catch a psi-gifted thief? The narrator hates and fears snakes above all. A girl he knows gags at the mere sight of a bird, since as a barefoot child she trod on a baby robin in the grass.

The narrator decides she is getting better at snakes, for this is the fourth since breakfast, and the roughest of the lot. A diamondback rattler lies coiled on the rug at his feet. His swipe fails, leaving the snake wrapped neatly round his forearm like a Western Union splice. He commands it to vanish, and it does not. Old Maragon, grand master of the Lodge, enters complaining. Readers get a psi-thief hunt, with snakes.
2477-the-circus-boys-on-the-mississippi-:
The Circus Boys go afloat with the big show on the Mississippi in this river volume, where showboats and river towns give their act a new stage. Edgar B. P. Darlington follows the young performers down the great river, through storms, landings, and rival shows. The Mississippi itself, with its traffic and lore, steals scenes.

The book's river flavor sets it apart in the series, and its adventures suit the setting. Young readers will enjoy the change of waters. It is a lively, colorful installment. River showboats carried whole circuses along the Mississippi in that era.
24922-the-honourable-mr-tawnish:
Jeffery Farnol published The Honourable Mr. Tawnish in Boston in 1913, with pictures by Charles E. Brock. The Georgian romp opens at The Chequers inn, runs through a flight of steps, a stirrup, and a stone, and meets a highwayman at the crossroads whose true identity surprises all.

Jack and Bentley, old Charterhouse friends, look back on a love they shared: both loved the same woman, she chose Jack, and she died young, leaving them Pen, now a woman grown. Christmas, a ring of steel, and old adages about love and honor fill the later chapters. Farnol tells it with high spirits and period color, in the style of his Broad Highway.
24954-pig-headed-sailor-men-from-the-str:
Louis Becke's sea stories from 'The Strange Adventure of James Shervinton,' published by T. Fisher Unwin in 1902, open with Captain Rosser of the barque Rimitara. His run from Sydney to Samoa by way of the Friendly Islands sets the stage for a race challenge from a smart new Tonga brigantine. The race is a contest of seamanship and pride between rival crews. Becke tells it with the detail of a man who knew the Pacific trade.

The mood darkens when the voyage ends in wreck, with boats capsizing near the shore and sailors fighting for their lives in sight of land. Pig-headed pride, the collection's theme, proves as dangerous as any reef. These are yarns of stubborn men and hard water, told without varnish and full of the South Seas.
25163-at-good-old-siwash:
George Fitch's At Good Old Siwash, published by Little, Brown in 1916, is a comic chronicle of college life at the fictional Siwash College. Fitch, a popular humorist, follows students through football seasons, fraternity initiations, and campus pranks.

Hero Ole Skjarsen, a Norwegian newcomer, scores touchdowns with rival players hanging on his legs and stumbles through initiations and Greek rivalries. Other chapters offer frappéd football, votes from women, and a funeral that flashes in the pan. The book's slang and high spirits made Siwash a byword for American college humor.
25590-the-silly-jelly-fish-told-in-engli:
B. H. Chamberlain tells this Japanese tale in English, published by Griffith Farran in London and Sydney. The Silly Jelly Fish opens with the King of the Dragons, till then a bachelor, deciding to marry a young dragonette just sixteen, lovely enough to wed a king.

Fishes great and small bring gifts, and feasting runs for days, until the young dragon queen falls ill within a month. Doctors dose her without success, and the story turns on a quest for a cure that only a jellyfish can supply. Chamberlain keeps the telling simple, comic, and suited to children.
25664-the-earliest-arithmetics-in-englis:
Robert Steele edits the earliest arithmetics in English for the Early English Text Society, extra series number 118, published by Oxford University Press in 1922 for 1916. His introduction notes how few English arithmetics existed before the sixteenth century.

Most people who needed even simple arithmetic before the mid fifteenth century knew Latin, where treatises abounded in manuscript. Until modern commerce grew, few needed more than addition and subtraction, and even advanced students in the thirteenth century might lack simple division. Texts include the Crafte of Nombrynge, counting by counters, and numbering by hand.
25750-colonial-born-a-tale-of-the-queens:
G. Firth Scott writes Colonial Born, a tale of the Queensland bush. He had written The Track of Midnight and The Romance of Australian Exploring. Sampson Low published the book in London. Percy F. S. Spence supplied six pictures. A horse and rider dashing out of smoke fronts the book.

Chapters open with the romance of Taylor's Flat, twenty years after, the belle of Birralong, and the rout of Boulder Creek. The sway of gold, the lady of Barellan, and the evolution of slaughter follow, with skinning the wild cat, chords and discords, and a race for gold. Scott dedicates the book to the original Ailleen.
2731-the-christmas-books-of-mr-m-a-titma:
William Makepeace Thackeray, as Mr. M. A. Titmarsh, gathers his Christmas books in this volume. Mrs. Perkins's Ball, Our Street, Dr. Birch and his Young Friends, and The Kickleburys on the Rhine lead to The Rose and the Ring, the history of Prince Giglio and Prince Bulbo.

The Mulligan of Ballymulligan opens Mrs. Perkins's Ball with a confession of ignorance about his own place, setting Thackeray's comic tone. The books mix satire, sentiment, and fairy tale, all meant for the holiday fireside. They show Thackeray at his most playful, and his most tender.
2768-the-paris-sketch-book-of-mr-m-a-tit:
William Makepeace Thackeray, as Mr. M. A. Titmarsh, sketches Paris in this volume, with a dedicatory letter and an advertisement to the first edition. An invasion of France, a caution to travelers, and the fetes of July open the tour.

The French school of painting, a gambler's death, Napoleon and his system, and the story of Mary Ancel follow, with Beatrice Merger and caricatures. Thackeray writes as a young Englishman abroad, satirical and curious. The book charms as a travel sketch, and as an early display of his eye. Thackeray's Paris bustles with painters, gamblers, and fetes.
27926-in-eastern-seas-or-the-commission-:
J. J. Smith of the Royal Navy wrote In Eastern Seas, the commission of H.M.S. Iron Duke, flagship in China from 1878 to 1883, printed at Devonport in 1883 and dedicated to his late shipmates. Smith says he wrote only to please his friends, at their suggestion, and claims no originality beyond that.

The narrative follows commissioning at Portsmouth, Gibraltar, Malta, the Suez Canal, Singapore, Hong Kong, Amoy, and Nagasaki, with notes on Chinese manners and Japanese towns. The book preserves a Victorian naval cruise in firsthand, unpretentious detail, including the Iron Duke aground at O'Kosiri.
2796-the-memoirs-of-mr-charles-j-yellowp:
William Makepeace Thackeray invented Charles Yellowplush, a footman who writes his own memoirs in gloriously misspelled English. The volume gathers linked comic episodes, including Miss Shum's husband, the amours of the gambler Deuceace, and Yellowplush's later jottings from Paris. The joke runs through every page, since the narrator reports high society while mangling its language.

Beneath the comedy, Thackeray uses his servant narrator to expose snobbery, gambling, and social climbing among his betters. Yellowplush misses nothing except his own spelling, and his plain view of fashionable life is sharper for it. The book rewards readers who enjoy satire told in a voice that never quite knows how funny it is.
27977-austral-english:
Edward E. Morris, professor of English, French, and German at the University of Melbourne, published Austral English in 1898, a dictionary of Australasian words, phrases, and usages, with Aboriginal-Australian and Maori words. The work began as help for the Oxford English Dictionary.

Morris explains that the book is not a slang dictionary, and he treats sources of new words, the law of Hobson-Jobson, classification, and quotations from books used as authorities. The dictionary remains a foundation for Australian English studies, recording a new nation's speech in its first century.
28019-birds-in-the-bush:
Bradford Torrey published Birds in the Bush in Boston with Houghton, Mifflin in 1893, in a sixth edition after an 1885 copyright. The essays begin on Boston Common, which Torrey admits is no ideal field for a bird student, being straitened and public, yet not without compensations.

Chapters cover bird-songs, character in feathers, the White Mountains, winter birds about Boston, an owl's head holiday, and a month's music. Torrey writes with a naturalist's patience and a literary ear, and the book remains a classic of American bird writing from the age before field guides.
29214-dialogues-in-french-and-english:
William Caxton printed these dialogues in French and English about 1483, adapted from a fourteenth-century dialogue book in French and Flemish. This Early English Text Society volume, extra series number 79, edits Caxton's printed text with an introduction, notes, and word-lists by Henry Bradley, joint editor of the New English Dictionary. It was published in 1900.

The dialogues taught travelers and traders to speak across languages, pairing French phrases with English equivalents. Bradley's notes and lists make the old text usable for students. Readers get a landmark of English printing and language learning, showing how a fifteenth-century printer helped English speakers talk to their French-speaking neighbors.
29876-death-wish:
Ned Lang wrote Death Wish, with pictures by Weiss. Its headnote warns that beside a spaceship in distress, going to hell in a handbasket is roomy and slow. The space freighter Queen Dierdre, a big, squat, scarred freighter on the Earth-Mars run, never caused anyone the least trouble. That, the tale says, should have warned Mr. Watkins, her engineer, who loved to say equipment fails bit by bit, or all at once.

Watkins, short, red-faced, and magnificently mustached, is foolishly infatuated with Dierdre, idealizing and humanizing her. Captain Somers, thin and meticulous, runs the ship with mechanical perfection, and Mr. Rajcik navigates. At Point Able the engines stop at the proper moment, and Somers frowns at his complex control board. Lang keeps the dread tight and the crew's pride sharp, in a brisk space disaster tale.
29885-the-cariboo-trail-a-chronicle-of-t:
Agnes C. Laut wrote The Cariboo Trail, a chronicle of the gold-fields of British Columbia, printed in Toronto in 1916. A frontispiece after a photograph shows the first Legislative Assembly of Vancouver Island, with J. W. McKay, J. D. Pemberton, and James Yates among its members. A map by Bartholomew shows the Cariboo country, and portraits of Sir James Douglas and Sir Matthew Baillie Begbie fill the plates.

Eight chapters carry the tale from the argonauts and the prospector to Cariboo itself and the overlanders. Crossing the mountains, Quesnel and Kamloops, and life at the mines follow, with the Cariboo Road to close. A bibliographical note and an index end the book. Laut writes a short, vivid history of a gold rush, its roads, its towns, and the men who sought its gold.
2989-garrison-s-finish:
W. B. M. Ferguson wrote Garrison's Finish as a romance of the racecourse, opening with a shattered idol. Garrison rolls a cigarette from Durham tobacco in the paddock, his reputation once as spotless as his even white teeth, now smiling cynically through a crowd that congregates without blending. The racecourse becomes a kaleidoscope of people betting fortune on speed, science, and stamina.

The plot turns on a burlesque engagement, property, and parents' blessings, as a woman refuses to elope and free her lover from a muddle unscathed. She accuses him of wanting her to suffer rather than himself. The novel mixes racing detail with melodrama, and it appeals to readers who enjoy Edwardian sporting fiction with a cynical hero.
3032-the-fathers-of-the-constitution-a-c:
Max Farrand wrote The Fathers of the Constitution, volume thirteen of the Chronicles of America series, published by Yale University Press in 1921. Chapters move from the treaty of peace through trade and industry, the Confederation, the Northwest Ordinance, darkness before dawn, the Federalist convention, and finishing the work, to the Union established. Farrand treats the Constitution as the product of crisis, not consensus.

The narrative shows Congress in despair over finances, as some states accepted proposals in full, seven in part, and four failed to act at all. All states except New York at last agreed to an impost, yet one refusal blocked the whole measure. Farrand's compact history remains a clear guide to how the framers built a federal government from confederation's failure.
30370-favourite-welsh-hymns-translated-i:
Joseph Morris, of Narberth, Pembrokeshire, formerly of Coward College, London, translates favourite Welsh hymns into English in a Carmarthen and London volume from 1854. From the top of the rocks I see him, the epigraph says, and from the hills I behold him, in the Welsh cry of a crowd in the mountains. Morris offers his translations to readers already at home in the originals' language and spirit, who would welcome their adaptation to changed circumstances.

He hopes the versions still carry some power to renew and sustain what the originals impressed on hearers. English Christians, too, may gain for the Church when diverse expressions of one spirit answer each other. A specimen of Welsh devotional song, with a few English originals included, illustrates its characteristic genius, its metres retained wherever possible, with an index of first lines at the end.
3067-hard-cash:
Charles Reade wrote Hard Cash as a matter-of-fact romance, fiction built on truths gathered by long, severe, systematic labor. Reade's preface lists volumes, pamphlets, journals, reports, blue books, manuscript narratives, letters, and living people sought out, examined, and cross-examined for each main topic. The madhouse scenes drew on that research, and the novel attacks private asylums and the law of lunacy.

The plot follows money, marriage, and madness, with a quack prescribing brandy and water after pain, claiming intoxication weakens the body's memory and expedites cure. A driver, not quite drunk enough to lose horse and vehicle, watches for a robber. Reade's indignation drives a long, absorbing novel that helped reform the treatment of the insane.
32527-the-adventures-of-alphonso-and-mar:
Set in Granada, this Spanish tale follows Marina, a seventeen-year-old orphan and heiress to an immense fortune. Her avaricious uncle Alonzo guards her closely, counting ducats by day and silencing serenades by night, because he plans to marry her to his own son Henriquez for her wealth.

Don Alphonso, a handsome captain of cavalry about twenty, loves Marina and courts her through letters and whispered talks at her lattice. Their secret correspondence grows despite the uncle's watch, and the story turns on whether love and cunning can outmatch a guardian who treats marriage as a bargain.
32654-project-hush:
William Tenn tells of a secret American effort to plant a permanent armed station on the Moon before any rival can get there. The narrator frets that the very name, Project Hush, invites the curiosity it must avoid, so the staff face extra checks on their dreams and thoughts.

After an unmanned craft reaches the Moon and fails, a crew lands near Mare Nubium and sets to work in a dome. The tale turns on secrecy itself: a mission so well hidden may leave its own men cut off, unheard, and unsure who, if anyone, will come for them.
32828-backlash:
Winston Marks tells of the Ollies, little immigrants from Sirius who come to Earth seeking asylum, in this story from Galaxy Science Fiction of January 1954, illustrated by Sibley. The fifty-six survivors of a shipwreck off the Maine coast take the commonest Earth names they can find, such as Johnson, Smith, and Jones.

Eager to please and everlastingly grateful, they offer humanity a gift beyond price: a custom-built domestic servant. Directors and householders are charmed by the tireless Soth. The prototype Soth obeys a first directive of his own: preserve the Willow Run Plant, and change production to Siths, the female counterparts of Soths.
32846-international-short-stories-englis:
William Patten edits a collection of famous English short stories, published in New York by P. F. Collier and Son with copyright 1910. The use of each copyrighted story was authorized by its author or representatives. Twenty-three stories fill the volume, from Scott to Borrow.

The contents open with Sir Walter Scott's The Two Drovers, set the day after Donne Fair among Highland cattle drovers. Thackeray, Lytton, Dickens, Wilkie Collins, and Samuel Lover follow, with Reade, Kipling, Stevenson, and Conan Doyle after them. Jacobs, Crockett, Anstey, Quiller-Couch, and Barrie bring the collection toward its close. Wells contributes The Stolen Body, and Marryat a great triangular duel.
33585-reply-of-the-philadelphia-brigade-:
The Philadelphia Brigade Association issued this March 1910 reply to Lieutenant Frank A. Haskell's narrative of the Battle of Gettysburg. At a September 1909 meeting, survivors heard letters from General Alexander S. Webb, who had commanded the brigade on July 1, 2, and 3, 1863, objecting to Haskell's account. The association unanimously resolved to answer what it called the narrative's astounding misstatements.

At issue is Haskell's claim, in a letter written days after the battle and later republished, about General Meade and the Army of the Potomac at Gettysburg. The reply argues the brigade's record from the testimony of its own officers and men. For Civil War readers, the pamphlet preserves a sharp veterans' dispute over credit, memory, and command on the battle's second and third days.
34131-butterflies-and-moths-british:
W. Furneaux wrote this guide to British butterflies and moths, with pictures. A note warns that many taxonomic names have changed since the book's first age, and that species names here often carry capitals, unlike current practice. No attempt has been made to update the names, so the book keeps its period form.

Furneaux describes British kinds with notes on form, habit, and haunts, aided by illustrations in the fuller version. The guide serves collectors and walkers who want to name what they see. It remains a useful, old-fashioned field book for British lepidoptera.
34534-britain-for-the-british:
Britain for the British is a socialist primer by Robert Blatchford, editor of the Clarion, published at London and Chicago in 1902. The book is dedicated to A M Thompson and the Clarion Fellowship. Its motto is its title, and its purpose is conversion.

At present, Blatchford argues, Britain belongs to a few of the British. The bulk of the people work as servants or hands for the owners. The contents build the case chapter by chapter. The unequal division of wealth opens it. The landlord's rights are set against the people's rights. What socialism is not, and what it is, stand at the centre. Competition and co-operation are weighed, then foreign trade and food. Can Britain feed herself gets a chapter. The need for a Labour Party closes the argument.
3464-tish:
Mary Roberts Rinehart gathers comic stories about Tish Carberry, a middle aged spinster who throws herself into motoring, camping, and war work with total confidence. The contents list Mind Over Motor, Like a Wolf on the Fold, The Simple Lifers, Tish's Spy, and My Country, Tish of Thee. In one scene Tish bumps home a winner at speed while her friends gasp.

Tish's charm lies in her refusal to act her age or her sex as her time defined them. She drives, camps, spies, and organizes, dragging her friends along and landing them in scrapes. Rinehart writes with warm humor and a quick pace. The stories suit readers who like funny, capable heroines and light tales of American life in the nineteen teens.
37091-a-song-of-the-english:
A Song of the English is a poem by Rudyard Kipling, printed at London by Hodder and Stoughton with pictures by Heath Robinson. The edition is reprinted from The Seven Seas, by leave of the first publishers, as a separate volume. A picture at the front shows the whisper, the vision, and the power arriving with the need.

The poem opens in a hymn voice: fair is our lot, goodly is our heritage, for the Lord has smote a pathway for the English to the ends of the earth. It bids the people hold the faith their fathers sealed and keep the law, swift in all obedience. Later songs take up the coastwise lights of England watching the ships of England go, with spindrift on the singers' brows.
37943-the-great-pike-s-peak-rush:
The Great Pike's Peak Rush, or Terry in the New Gold Fields, by Edwin L Sabin, was published by Thomas Y Crowell Company at New York in 1917. The place and time are the Pike's Peak country of the Rocky Mountains in 1859.

The cast lists Terry Richards off to the gold fields, his partner Harry Revere, and the tender-foot Stantons. Sol Judy is a Forty-niner, Pine Knot Ike is not so tough after all, and Shep is ready for anything. Horace Greeley of the New York Tribune appears among the busy folk thronging the gulches and young Denver City.
38341-the-lash:
The Lash, a novel by Olin Lyman, was published at Boston in 1909. Badger issued it from the Gorham Press with copyright in that year. Lyman also wrote The Trail of the Grand Seigneur, the title page notes. A star chamber session opens the contents as chapter one of the tale.

An arrival, Micky, and fists and the man follow in the chapter list. The ironworkers ball, and Maisie, fills the fifth chapter of the story. The web, loneliness, and an evening call build the middle of the contents. Not on the programme and the little red devil mark the turn toward crisis. Mill town labour strife and a love plot give this forgotten novel its drive.
38349-where-there-is-nothing-being-volum:
Where There Is Nothing is the first volume of Plays for an Irish Theatre, by Yeats. Bullen published it in London in 1903. The volume opens with a dedication of the first two volumes of the series to Lady Gregory.

Yeats tells her that the plays are in part her own. As a boy, he writes, he used to wander about Rosses Point and Ballisodare, listening to old songs and stories. He wrote down what he heard and made poems of the stories, or put them into The Celtic Twilight. That is how he began to write in the Irish way. Then he went to London to earn his living, spending part of every year in Ireland. His other books are listed in front: The Secret Rose, The Wind Among the Reeds, The Shadowy Waters, and Ideas of Good and Evil.
38388-a-bride-from-the-bush:
Bride from the Bush is a novel by Ernest William Hornung. Collins issued it in London and Glasgow in clear type. A front plate shows the heroine fresh and buoyant on a summer morning. Chapters open with a letter from Alfred and a homecoming in style. Pins and needles, a taste of her quality, and notes compared follow.

Granville weighs the situation, and Richmond Park hosts a key scene. Gran's revenge and a Latin headed chapter, E Tenebris, raise the stakes. An Australian bride in an English home gives the tale its friction. Manners, pride, and love collide as bush frankness meets town polish. Hornung, famed for Raffles, here works a lighter, domestic vein.
39726-the-rolliad-in-two-parts-probation:
The Rolliad is a work of political satire in verse, first aimed at the government of the younger Pitt. This file holds the twenty-first edition, printed in London in 1799, revised and enlarged by the original authors. The book pretends to print criticisms on itself before the satire begins. Its main device is a contest: politicians are made to offer probationary odes for the laureateship.

The odes are assigned to real public men, lords, baronets, and members of Parliament, each parodying its supposed author's character. Political eclogues precede them, with names such as Margaret Nicholson, the woman who tried to stab the king. Miscellanies follow: epigrams, anecdotes of Pitt, and a piece called This is the House that George Built. The Rolliad began in newspaper verses and grew by accretion. It remains one of the sharpest satires of Georgian politics.
40515-elijah-the-tishbite-miscellaneous-:
Elijah the Tishbite is the fifth volume of the miscellaneous writings of C H Mackintosh, published by Loizeaux Brothers of New York. First published in 1898, it is seen in the tenth printing of 1960. The volume gathers devotional papers with a long study of Elijah's life.

The first paper, God's Fulness for an Empty Vessel, reads Samuel's chapters on the ark and draws one rule: the fulness of God waits on an empty vessel. Man must reach the end of himself, bad self and good self alike, before grace can flow in. Other papers treat the divine titles, the discipline of the assembly, and the Christian's mission. Epaphras stands for the service of prayer, and The Three Crosses runs to thirty-five pages. A letter to a friend on eternal punishment, Israel and the Nations, and Saul of Tarsus show the range.
40550-plain-english:
Plain English is a grammar book by Marian Wharton, published in 1917 by the People's College at Fort Scott, Kansas. Its motto is set on the title page: for the education of the workers by the workers. A quote from Debs stands at the front on the power of plain speech. The voice of the oppressed, he says, is the most strong eloquence on earth. The lessons then run in order through the parts of speech. Language study and nouns and verbs come first.

Verbs get the fullest treatment, with their time forms, helpers, and common errors. Pronouns, adjectives, and the rest follow in turn. Each part is taught in short, clear steps, with speech in view. The book was made for working men and women who meant to speak and write with force. It joins school grammar to the platform of labour.
41448-the-oppressed-english:
The Oppressed English is a wartime essay book by Ian Hay, printed in 1917. Hay had written The First Hundred Thousand and Getting Together before. Doubleday, Page and Company brought the book out in New York. Hay signs himself with his full name, Ian Hay Beith, on the rights page. As a Scotsman, he opens by giving the English his deep sympathy.

In comic papers the Englishman stands stupid, proud, and thick-skinned, he says. In fact, Hay argues, he serves as whipping-boy of the whole empire. When mails are held or blacklists drawn, the blame falls on England alone. No one thunders at France, and seldom at Great Britain, in such rows. Schoolchildren in Germany greet their teacher with a curse on England. Yet wins by English regiments get called British wins in the reports. Hay presses the Scotsman's case for fair play in names.
41544-leadwork-old-and-ornamental-and-fo:
Leadwork, old and ornamental and for the most part English, is a study by Lethaby, printed by Macmillan at London and New York in 1893. A quote from Viollet-le-Duc stands at the front, praising medieval leadwork as wrought like colossal goldsmith's work, with forms exactly fitted to the material. Twenty sections, richly pictured, cover the craft whole.

The sections run from material and craftsmanship through a historical sketch to lead coverings, spires, domes, and roofs. Lead coffins, fonts, inscriptions, statues, fountains, cisterns, gutters, and pipe heads each get their place. Lethaby notes the low repute of plumbing in his day and sets out to show lead as a true art material with a long English past.
41721-the-crimson-flash:
Roy Snell wrote The Crimson Flash, published by Reilly and Lee in Chicago in 1922 as one of its Mystery Stories for Boys. The hero is Johnny Thompson, once a lightweight boxing champion, now set to guard work. The tale opens under the big top of a mammoth three-ring circus.

Eight trained elephants stand in line while brass horns blare. Marjory and Margaret MacDonald, millionaire twins just past ten, press against the rope at their first circus. When the foremost elephant reaches a trunk toward them, Johnny springs forward, but he is too slow to stop a sharp snap and an angry snort. Chapters promise a bunco-steerer, a tiger, and the wreck of the circus. A black cat and a character named Pant thread through Snell's circus mystery.
42166-the-poems-of-sappho-an-interpretat:
John Myers O'Hara made The Poems of Sappho, an interpretative rendition into English, at Portland in 1910. Lines from Maurice Thompson and from Swinburne stand at the front of the book. Thompson asks who shall break the wax of mystery from those priceless jars. The wine, he says, was pressed in a garden in Mitylene, twenty-five centuries ago. Swinburne's lines show Aphrodite drawn by doves, looking back to Lesbos.

The verse opens with The Muses, a call for the goddesses to leave the golden house of God. Sapphic stanzas beg for song like sunglow on the breast and brow. O'Hara does not give a bare, word-for-word crib of the Greek scraps. He builds full English poems that catch Sappho's fire, love, and grief. Readers get the famed singer of Lesbos in lush, song-like form.
43059-rumanian-bird-and-beast-stories-re:
Gaster rendered these Rumanian bird and beast stories into English for the Folk-Lore Society in 1915. A text from Job heads the book: ask the beasts, and they shall teach thee. Gaster, a rabbi and scholar, held high office in several learned societies named on his title page.

The book is dedicated by permission to Queen Elisabeth of Rumania, called Carmen Sylva. To her the soul of the Rumanian people is as an open book, the dedication says. The forests are silent in his preface's sad image, yet the tales keep the voices of bird and beast that peasants heard in them for ages.
43465-the-kangaroo-hunters-or-adventures:
The Kangaroo Hunters, or Adventures in the Bush, is a boys' adventure book by Anne Bowman. Porter and Coates published it in Philadelphia. Bowman had written Esperanza, The Castaways, and The Young Exiles. Her preface, signed from Richmond in October 1858, defends adventure tales for the young. Youth, she argues, craves food for the imagination. Even nursery rhymes charm by their improbability.

The boy who leaves Ali Baba and Sindbad, she says, turns to Robinson Crusoe. A hundred tales on the Crusoe model followed it. Bowman aims to describe the marvellous works of creation. Her books, she promises, do not profess to be true, though composed of truths. The contents open with the rector and the soldier. The Mayburn family, a mission to India, and orphans follow. Australia supplies the stage and the title hunt. A frontispiece shows a kangaroo seizing the narrator in its arms.
4389-roughing-it-in-the-bush:
Susanna Moodie wrote this classic account of settler life in the Canadian bush, dedicating it to her sister Agnes Strickland, author of Lives of the Queens of England. Moodie came to Upper Canada with hopes of a comfortable farm, and found instead clearing, cold, debt, and the hard labor of bush life.

Her chapters mix narrative, sketch, and verse, with scenes of neighbors, servants, and the forest itself. Different editions vary in names, spelling, and chapters, and this text aims to be readable and inclusive rather than matching one paper edition. The book remains a foundation of Canadian literature, frank about hardship and proud of endurance.
4494-the-tale-of-chloe-an-episode-in-the:
George Meredith tells this short episode from the world of Beau Beamish, a wit whose sharp tongue sets the tone in fashionable society. Chloe, once toasted as the queen of a festival meeting, is now dead, and the tale looks back at her beauty, her gifts, and her fall from favour. Dukes, dairymaids, and ballads all play a part, as high society tries to dress up an awkward marriage in fine language.

Beamish gives the rustic bride her mock title, the Duke of Dewlap, and the joke saves a great house from open scorn. Beneath the comedy, Meredith probes reputation, class, and the price women paid for a past that men could laugh away. Readers get a witty, bittersweet story about fame, gossip, and the gap between a ballad and a real life.
45338-through-bosnia-and-herzegovina-wit:
Through Bosnia and Herzegovina with a Paint Brush is a travel book by Mrs Whitwell, printed at Darlington. She had writ Spain As We Found It and a Corsica book of the same kind. The sketches began as the notes of a holiday in a land off the beaten track. By the time of print, the land had come to the front of Europe's mind. Austria's move to take the provinces, and Bulgaria's claim of independence, fill her new preface.

A street in Sarajevo stands in a plate at the front. Whitwell tours the provinces with her brush, making pictures as she goes. No book on these lands drawn from the brush had come before, she believes. Dalmatia has its books, but Bosnia and Montenegro lack them. Her tour gives towns, dress, and wild hills in word and image. It is a holiday book that history overtook.
46284-my-austrian-love-the-history-of-th:
Maxime Provost's My Austrian Love, the history of an English composer in Vienna, was issued by the Iris Publishing Company of London. The title page announces that it was written in the trenches, by himself. Front matter praises his earlier novel Montorel in clippings from the Times, the Athenaeum, and the Glasgow Herald. A note tells readers that many personages are genuine: Hammer, Provost hints, is Anton Bruckner, the famous antagonist of Brahms. Twelve numbered chapters and an introduction make the book.

The introduction crosses into Austria on the railway bridge over the Salzach, where Bavarian territory ceases. Salzburg's fortress and spires strike the traveler more than the border fact. An irascible Frenchman in the carriage flies into a rage at the cry of all change. He insists he does not have to change trains. The composer narrator mutters about custom regulations.
46543-nature-books-popular-and-scientifi:
Catalogue number twenty-four, for the season nineteen ten to eleven, lists nature books sold by the Franklin Bookshop in Philadelphia. Samuel Rhoads ran the shop at 920 Walnut Street. The list claims more than two thousand titles on beasts, plants, rocks, and sport. Most are out of print works, each with a price and a short note on state and rarity.

The list opens with books on mammals, from studies of bats and bison to Audubon's large plates of four footed beasts. One Audubon set in six bound parts is priced at $225.00, while short papers cost cents. Notes flag first prints, fine copies, and scarce runs. The catalogue serves buyers who hunt old science books by mail.
46803-diary-of-richard-cocks-volume-1-ca:
Richard Cocks kept this diary as cape-merchant of the English factory in Japan from 1615 to 1622, and his letters home travel with it. Edward Maunde Thompson edited the volume for the Hakluyt Society, whose first series carried it as number 66 in 1883.

The preface explains why the English settlement in Japan failed. The depot stood on Firando, a small island in the far west with a poor anchorage, far from Miako and Yedo. The Dutch, looked to as allies against the Spaniards and Portuguese, turned into rivals who undersold the English and starved them out. Branch factories were opened, but privileges shrank until the English were shut to Firando alone.
47194-humorous-hits-and-how-to-hold-an-a:
Grenville Kleiser gathered short funny pieces for the platform, in a thirteenth form of a book first printed at New York and London in 1908. His How to Speak in Public is named as his on the title page. A first word owns the ground of the work. Twelve years of stage work stand behind it.

Hundreds of public readings, before crowds of all kinds, taught him what lands. The encore fiend, he says, lurks at each show and must be fed. Stock books of pieces, made by men who never faced a crowd, fail that test. His hints treat voice, pause, gesture and feeling. School teachers, toast speakers and home readers share the gain.
47408-folk-lore-and-legends-english:
Folk-lore and Legends: English was printed by W W Gibbings at London in 1890. Its first note, signed C J T, mourns a loss. The old tales die fast as folk trade old myths for new, and the verse of life fades in the fight to live. The editor sought the best of the store and took the nursery tales from the first prints he could find, with as light a hand as he could keep.

Joseph Ritson's long piece on fairies leads the book. Then come Jack and the Giants, Jack and the Beanstalk, and Thomas Hickathrift. The Wise Men of Gotham play the fool, the Worm of Lambton coils, and a Yorkshire boggart prowls. King Arthur's tales and the cobbler who cheated the Devil close the roll. Folk fans get a stout hoard of the old fireside England.
48012-diary-of-richard-cocks-volume-2-ca:
Richard Cocks keeps a day book of the English factory in Japan in volume two of his diary. Edward Maunde Thompson edited it for the Hakluyt Society. Burt Franklin reprinted it at New York.

Cocks was cape-merchant, the chief of the factory, from 1615 to 1622. The year 1618 opens with bills of exchange. One bill from the King of Firando's man runs to 3000 tais. Gunpowder, cloth, and money lent fill the page. At midnight Cocks boards the junk for Cochy himself. He carries bread, a venison pasty, roast beef, and Spanish wine. Mr Eaton turns nine hidden passengers out of the mariners' cabins. The diary's plain entries on gifts, junks, and kings give rare ground-level sight of early trade with Japan.
48080-the-chariot-of-the-flesh:
Hedley Peek's novel The Chariot of the Flesh, published at London and New York in 1897, takes its title from a verse in The Secret of Death. In the verse the body is the chariot, the will its charioteer, the mind the reins and the senses the steeds. Peek dedicates the book to the Rev S A Tipple, his friend and teacher of thirty years. An Emerson line stands at the head of the first part.

The narrator, released from a promise of secrecy after nearly eleven years, tells the strange history of Alan Sydney of Anstead in Surrey. Sydney fascinates, repels and puzzles him, seeming to hold several individualities inside one person.
48685-spinster-of-this-parish:
Spinster of This Parish is a novel by W B Maxwell, issued at New York in nineteen twenty two. A list of the author's novels stands at the front, among them The Mirror and the Lamp. A note by the author heads the tale. It says neither the persons nor the events of the story are drawn from real life.

Names of the living or the dead appear only where leaving them out seemed impossible, the note adds. Chapter one opens with a young girl's odd impulse. Little Mildred Parker seeks counsel, or at least sympathy, from Miss Verinder. The need to open her heart to somebody lay behind the step, the narrator says. Miss Verinder was really only an acquaintance of Mildred's parents. The spinster of the title watches life at fifty and weighs what age means for a woman.
49249-folk-lore-and-legends-russian-and-:
Folk-Lore and Legends, Russian and Polish, was published at London by Gibbings in 1890 as one of a uniform series of dainty little books. The editor draws the tales from Russian chap books and from collectors such as Afanasief, Erben, Wojcicki, and Glinski. Some stories came from abroad, he admits, but Russia and Poland made them their own.

Contents mix the two lands tale by tale: The Poor Man and the Judge, Snyegurka the snow maiden, Emelyan the Fool, Ilija of Murom, the evil eye, and the stolen heart. The Times, quoted on the series page, said these books transport us into a romantic world.
49324-the-authoress-of-the-odyssey-where:
The Authoress of the Odyssey, by Samuel Butler, was issued at New York in 1922. Dutton printed this edition of Butler's famous argument. Nausicaa stands in the frontispiece. The long subtitle states the programme: where and when she wrote, who she was, her use of the Iliad, and how the poem grew under her hands. Butler had published parts in England and Italy over six years. Pieces ran in the Athenaeum in 1892 and in Sicilian journals after. Local students at Trapani and Calatafimi helped him correct and add.

A legal motto heads the book: no single fact convicts, but a chain of facts leaves no escape. Butler notes that no scholar answered his letters. Silence, he implies, is not refutation. His case: a young woman of Trapani in Sicily wrote the Odyssey.
4954-laicus-or-the-experiences-of-a-laym:
Lyman Abbott's Laicus follows a layman who comes to the country parish of Wheathedge, about sixty miles north of New York up the Hudson. The village sits in a beautiful site on the river, and the narrator, writing from his library, watches morning sun gild the spires below him as he begins his story.

How he happened to go to Wheathedge, and what he found in parish life, churchgoing, and neighborly talk, forms the book's substance. Abbott writes as a thoughtful lay observer rather than a clergyman. Readers get a gentle portrait of American church life, where faith shows in daily conduct more than in doctrine.
50883-narrative-and-critical-history-of-:
Houghton, Mifflin printed this second volume of the Narrative and Critical History of America in 1886. More than three hundred plates fill the book. The Spanish arms of Herrera's old title page grace its own title, a sign of its theme.

The editor opens with the written sources of early Spanish-American history. Columbus and his discoveries take the first chapter, by the editor's own hand. Plates show Columbus's armour, his parting from Ferdinand and Isabella, and his ships. His own handwriting, his arms, and the house where he died all stand in the list. A critical essay then weighs the finds, in the set's learned manner.
50987-narrative-and-critical-history-of-:
Justin Winsor, librarian of Harvard University, edits the Narrative and Critical History of America, and this third volume covers English explorations and settlements in North America from 1497 to 1689. Copyrighted in 1884, the volume carries more than 240 illustrations, including early maps in facsimile. Charles Deane writes on the voyages of the Cabots, with a critical essay.

Edward E Hale treats Hawkins and Drake, adding a critical essay on Drake's Bay, and Charles C Smith covers explorations to the north-west. Editor's notes on sources and the Zeno influence on early cartography accompany the narratives. Autographs of kings, queens and explorers are reproduced beside the maps.
51079-ned-bob-and-jerry-at-boxwood-hall-:
Clarence Young wrote Ned, Bob and Jerry at Boxwood Hall, or The Motor Boys as Freshmen. Cupples and Leon put out the New York book at sixty cents a volume. It stands in the second series of the Motor Boys books. The front plate shows Bob crossing home plate with his run. Jerry is not far behind him in the baseball scene.

The series list runs from The Motor Boys to Motor Boys on Road and River. Jack Ranger and Racer Boys books by Young stand in the same pages. At Boxwood Hall the three friends enter school life as freshmen. Chapters in the wider set promise a professor's dilemma and time in the gymnasium. An aeroplane, a postponed examination, and school games fill the boys' year. Young gives school sport and scrapes in the brisk mode of his line.
51209-babes-in-the-bush:
Babes in the Bush is an Australian novel by Rolf Boldrewood, issued by Macmillan in 1900. Boldrewood had won his name with Robbery Under Arms and The Miner Right. Contents open with fresh fields and pastures new, then the first camp of the settlers. The new home follows, with Henry O Desmond of Badajos entering at chapter four.

Emigrant families in the Australian bush face fire, flood, loss, and hard neighbours. Children lost or in peril give the old title phrase its bush meaning here. Boldrewood writes from years of colonial life as magistrate and pastoral veteran. Australian literature keeps him as the classic novelist of the squatting age.
52451-living-bayonets-a-record-of-the-la:
Living Bayonets, a record of the last push by Coningsby Dawson, was published in New York in 1919. A motto heads the book: our spirits are living bayonets, and the ideals in our hearts are more deadly to the foe than any man-made weapons. The record is built from letters home, the first dated from France on April 14, 1917.

Dawson tells how letters reached him at midnight as he climbed into a bunk lately held by a German. He lit a candle and feasted on home gossip. News that the United States had joined as an ally made him almost gay. Cash and factories would help at once, he writes, and the moral blow to Germany was the greatest wound yet to her spirit.
52806-the-life-and-adventures-of-guzman-:
The life and adventures of Guzman d'Alfarache, the Spanish Rogue, translated from Le Sage's French edition by John Henry Brady, in a second edition of 1823 revised and considerably improved. The translator thanks his reviewers and owns to softening the parts complained of as too significant.

His preface traces the rogue's fame: hardly a language in Europe knows not Guzman. An English version by several hands appeared in 1708, with an older one of 1634 praised in verses by Ben Jonson. Jonson calls the hero a Spanish Proteus, formed with the world's wit. This first of three volumes presents the picaresque classic freshly dressed for Regency readers. Spanish literature's great rogue gets an English advocate.
52938-the-life-and-adventures-of-guzman-:
A rogue's tale fills this volume: The Life and Adventures of Guzman d'Alfarache, or the Spanish Rogue. Brady rendered it from an older French version, and it was printed at London in 1823 in a second edition, corrected and much improved. The hosted text is the second of three volumes. Chapter thirteen opens it in mid-career.

Guzman has served a cook faithfully and been turned out of doors for a trifling offence, as the great, he notes, treat far weightier servants every day. Stop moralizing, he tells himself, and get back to the basket: the begging trade consoles him, as eloquence consoled one Greek orator and stratagems another. All the gains of his knaveries have gone as lightly as they came, and with a finer suit of clothes he is no better off than before. Before buying a new basket he means to offer his service to other cooks.
53081-the-life-and-adventures-of-guzman-:
The Life and Adventures of Guzman d Alfarache is a tale of a rogue of Spain, in three books. The form here is book three, in a second form put out in London in 1823. John Henry Brady put it into English from the French form of Le Sage. The text was made sound and much made new in this form.

Part 35 finds Guzman at the court of the Grand Duke, where a lady falls for him. The Grand Duchess had just borne a prince and lay in rest. Feasts ran each day at the palace, and all folk of rank came to join them. Knights at his inn, of the first rank of the land, came to Florence for the sport.
53521-oysters-and-fish:
Oysters and Fish is a cookery book by Thomas Murrey, issued at New York in 1888. Murrey had written many small cookery books before, and they crowd the title page: fifty soups, fifty salads, breakfast dainties, puddings, and more. He dedicates this little work to the inventor of a close top gas stove, and to the gas company men who backed him.

The contents open with the oyster itself, its season, and oysters out of season. Keeping oysters in the shell and the food of the oyster follow in the heads. From that start the book treats its two subjects in the plain recipe manner of Murrey's series. Economy in fuel and labour in the home, praised in the dedication, is the spirit of the whole line.
53862-loughton-essex-a-brief-account-of-:
William Chapman Waller wrote Loughton, Essex, a brief account of the manor and parish. The paper was read in 1903 and reported in the Loughton Gazette. One hundred copies were reprinted in October 1913, priced at sixpence. Waller hints at a fuller account in a volume of only twelve copies, held at the Guildhall Library and the British Museum. The story of Loughton reaches back before Domesday Book.

In 1062, four years before the Conqueror came, King Edward confirmed a great gift of lands to the monastery at Waltham. Harold, son of Godwin, had made the gift to his canons. The charter names three estates whose bounds are given in Anglo-Saxon, not Latin. Lukinton, Tippedene, and Aelwartun are the places now known as Loughton, Debden, and Alderton. Waller writes parish history from the charters up.
55057-daily-lesson-plans-in-english:
Daily Lesson Plans in English is a teacher's manual by Caroline Griffin, copyrighted in 1914 by the Educational Publishing Company of Boston. The book lays out a year of daily lessons for young children, arranged by month and week, beginning with September's first year work. Each day gets a short, concrete exercise in language, observation and play.

The first week shows the method. On Monday the teacher shows a sunflower and asks the children to name other yellow flowers, then blue ones, then red. On Tuesday the class acts out Hey Diddle Diddle, with children as cat, fiddle, cow, moon, dish and spoon. Wednesday is for writing names and addresses; Thursday asks what colour sunshine is and what rain does for the trees; Friday has the children name everything they can see in the schoolroom. Later weeks add cleanliness talks, the flag and its stripes, and Mother Goose recitations.
55169-life-and-lillian-gish:
Life and Lillian Gish, by Albert Bigelow Paine, is a life of the film actress Lillian Gish, published in New York in 1932. Paine went to live in her household to write it.

The opening pages stress how hard Gish is to know. A wall of reserve, friends say, hides her from all but those who share her daily life. Chapter heads trace her path from a girl child born with a caul through years as a little trouper on the road. Mary Pickford appears in the story, and so does the great stage actress Sarah Bernhardt. Massillon days and the end of the road follow. The book covers her rise from travelling theatre to the heights of silent film.
56100-ten-years-of-missionary-work-among:
Missionary Eells of the American Missionary Association wrote this account of ten years at Skokomish, Washington Territory, from 1874 to 1884. The book came out in Boston in 1886. In his preface, Eells quotes a call for missions to be plainly 'written up,' so that churches can see a field's need, cost, prospects and methods.

Newspaper columns, he argues, do not give that full picture. Books from the foreign field had raised interest abroad, and home missions needed the same treatment. His ten years among the Skokomish Indians supply names, work and daily detail meant to win support and hold it.
56410-ruby-a-story-of-the-australian-bus:
Ruby, a story of the Australian bush, is a tale by Molly Jamieson, printed at London under the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge. Jamieson also wrote Jack, At Sunset, and Molly and I. A verse from Carlyle stands at the front: love not pleasure, love God. The contents run to ten chapters, from an Australian Christmas to a chapter for Wat's sake.

The tale opens on Christmas Day in the bush, under a blazing sun on parched ground, far from the Christmases of Scotland or England. A creek dances past the station garden toward a river half a mile away, and blue bush stretches to the horizon. Ruby waits for a guest while the pudding cools, a small worry on a vast, hot day.
56453-the-egregious-english:
Angus McNeill published this sharp satire in 1903, with a copyright date of 1902. Its first chapter, 'Apollo,' mocks the Englishman's calm belief that he stands at the head of the world. McNeill argues that pride, ease and sure faith in his own worth mark the type, even in trouble, when he still trusts he will muddle through.

Later chapters take up one type at a time. The sportsman, the man of business, the journalist, the soldier, the church, the politician and the man-about-town all get their turn. Drink, food, law, schools, the Stock Exchange and love are treated too, in a brisk, teasing style.
56678-turgenev-in-english:
Turgenev in English is a checklist of works by and about the Russian novelist, issued in 1962. The New York Public Library published the volume in New York that year. Yachnin and Stam compiled the checklist for the library in its pages. Slonim wrote an introductory essay, Turgenev Revisited, for the volume in its front.

Contents divide the book into a preface, the essay, and the lists themselves in order. Works by Turgenev are split into collected editions and selected stories and plays in the list. Separately published works and pieces in anthologies and periodicals follow in the contents. The book records a century of translation, from the first English versions of the Sportsman Sketches to the modern versions of Fathers and Sons. Bibliographies of this kind are the quiet machinery of scholarship, and this one served students of Russian literature in English for a generation.
56693-the-boy-in-the-bush:
The Boy in the Bush is a tale of Australian life by the late Richard Rowe, printed in London in 1885. Rowe had also written Roughing It and The Deserted Ship. Four artists drew the plates, and a front plate shows a dog bristling like a porcupine.

Twelve chapters open with Venus and Warrigal, then a trip up a sunny creek and a cave of the red hand. Later heads treat snakes, a lost girl named Maggie, and an Australian drought and flood. A bush grave and the old convict times deepen the tale. The close brings pioneering and a gold rush. One note in a boy handwriting demands a chestnut mare by the next day, on pain of theft. Boys got the bush in all its heat and peril.
56827-whitewash:
Whitewash is a novel by Horace Annesley Vachell, published by Doran in New York in 1920. Vachell also wrote The Soul of Susan Yellam and Quinney's. The contents list twelve chapters of village and family life. Lady Selina Chandos opens the tale at page nine. Henry Grimshaw and Cupid Speeds His Shafts follow. Chiefly Concerning Cicely and Tiddy Appears come next in the list. Grimshaw Returns and Tiddy and Cicely fill the middle.

Pearls of Dew, Timothy Farleigh, and Under the Village Tree follow. Revolution and Reconstruction close the contents as a pair. The first chapter shows Lady Selina laying down her quill pen. She smiles pensively as the tale begins in her parlour. Her mother taught her to smile for the marriage market. That mother had half a dozen dowerless daughters to place. Vachell opens a comedy of manners with that smile.
56900-aspects-of-plant-life-with-special:
Aspects of Plant Life, with special reference to the British flora, is a botany book by Robert Lloyd Praeger in the Nature Lover's Series. The Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge published it in London in 1921, with Macmillan in New York. Praeger had written Open-Air Studies in Botany and a flora of the west of Ireland. A coloured frontispiece shows desert plants.

Chapters treat plant associations and plant migration after an opening on Farleton Fell. Coral root, bell-flower, geranium, and violet fruits show how seeds travel, with a diagram of the fall of seeds. Later chapters treat the inter-relations of plants and animals and plant structures, from burrowing lichens to leaf mosaics. Plants and man comes next, then past and present, where slime moulds and the maidenhair tree appear. A closing chapter picks out interesting British plant groups, among them the great butterwort.
57230-the-golden-boys-along-the-river-al:
The Golden Boys Along the River Allagash, published in 1923, is one of Wyman's Golden Boys stories for boys of twelve to sixteen. Bob and Jack, the golden boys, start stuck on a lake with a motor boat engine that will not fire. Gas and spark test fine, yet the flywheel only coughs. Their Maine woods holiday begins with grit and jokes.

The chapters bring in their friend Rex and the guide Kernertok, who reads huge tracks no one can name. A cry in the night, a lost boy and wild cats raise the stakes. A siege and a rescue close the trip. The book mixes woodcraft, motors and steady friendship.
57442-royalty-in-all-ages-the-amusements:
Royalty in All Ages, by T F Thiselton Dyer, was printed in London in 1903, with six etched portraits from old prints. Dyer writes on the play, whims, skills, and frolics of the kings and queens of Europe. A portrait of Queen Elizabeth stands near the front.

Twenty or more chapters sort royal fun by kind, from royalty at play and royal revelry to royal food lovers and dancing monarchs. Other heads treat the hunt, masks, kings in disguise, card play, and the turf. Later parts cover court dwarfs, royal pets, royal jokes, and court jesters and fools. Dyer packs the book with tales of odd, grand, and human acts at court. Readers who like crown lore told light will find rich store here.
57958-index-of-the-pg-works-of-voltaire-:
