The index was compiled by David Widger for Project Gutenberg readers. It lists the twelve volumes of Voltaire in English held by the project. The works named include A Philosophical Dictionary, Zadig, Candide, Micromegas and Letters on England.

The bulk of this first volume gives the contents of the Philosophical Dictionary, volume one. Its entries run from A, B, C, or Alphabet through Abbé, Abraham, Abuse of Words, Academy, Adam, Adultery, Alchemy, Alkoran, Alexander, Allegories, Angels, Apostles, Aristotle, Atheism and Avarice. The B and C parts run on in the same way, from Babel and Bacon to Caesar, Cannibals, Cato, Christianity and Church. The index is a finding tool: it lets a reader see at a glance the span of Voltaire's short essays on faith, history and thought before opening the full text.
58153-the-cambrian-directory-1800-or-cur:
The Cambrian Directory, printed at Salisbury in 1800, gives quick sketches of the Welsh territories for travelers. The author hides his name, with a verse at the front on great writers who do the same. A chart in the book shows the best route at one view.

The chart also lists the best inns, the distances, and the sights most worth a stop. The book is given, with thanks, to the kind and open hearted folk of Wales. Its writer calls himself an old bachelor in his address to the Welsh. He owns that he does not always take the beaten track. Road users of 1800 got a light, handy guide to Welsh towns, inns, and views in one small book.
59216-the-courtship-of-miles-standish:
The Courtship of Miles Standish, by Henry Longfellow, appears here in the Collection of Masterpieces, with original illustrations by Walter Russell. Stokes copyrighted the edition at New York in 1901. The poem is written in long, rolling lines and set in Plymouth, in the Old Colony days.

Part one introduces the captain. Miles Standish strides to and fro in his dwelling, clad in doublet and hose and boots of Cordovan leather. His weapons hang in shining array on the chamber walls: cutlass, corslet of steel, and his sword of Damascus. He tells of the breastplate that once saved his life in a skirmish. The dent of the Spanish bullet, fired point blank at his heart, shows in front. Beside him sits John Alden, his friend, writing with speed at a pine table. Fair haired and azure eyed, Alden was the youngest of the men who came in the May Flower.
5988-old-french-romances-done-into-engli:
William Morris renders old French romances into English, with an introduction by Joseph Jacobs. Many readers first met the realm of romance through a little crimson volume of the Bibliothèque Elzevirienne. Its last pages hold the cante-fable of Aucassin et Nicolete, praised by Pater and Englished by Lang.

The same volume holds four other tales, equally charming in their way, which Morris now makes part of English letters. His versions first appeared in three Kelmscott Press issues, eagerly sought by lovers of good books. Morris reproduces the tone, color, and charm of the Middle Ages in living prose.
60291-bramble-bush:
Bramble Bush is a science fiction story by Alan Nourse. It was printed in Worlds of If Science Fiction in August 1957. The rhyme gives the story its title and its sting.

The tale opens at the Hoffman Center on a morning. Doctor David Lessing comes into his office to find his field director, Jack Dorffman, waiting with a boy. Dorffman looks as though he has been running all night, with dark pouches under his eyes. The boy, he says, is driving him mad. The lad has gone completely haywire. No one has been able to get near him for three weeks. Now, at six in the morning, the boy says he is leaving the Farm. Lessing sighs, sits down behind his desk, and asks what is wrong.
60846-a-great-day-for-the-irish:
A Great Day for the Irish is a short tale of ships and strict checks. Lightner wrote it for a pulp book of the year 1960. Bridget Kelly stands at the foot of a rocket lift at the start. She is glad, for once, to be a guest and not the check hand.

All goods had been checked and stowed when the tale opens. She grins as a fine dame's bloom is tossed in the trash. A man's small flower goes the same way in the next breath. Earth keeps a strict guard at its ports, the tale tells us. Bugs and plagues from the stars must be kept off the home world. The watch dogs of that guard must be watched in their turn. That twist, flagged at the head, is the heart of the tale.
61161-the-saxons-in-england-volume-1-of-:
The Saxons in England, volume one of two, is a past of the realm of that folk till the great conquest. John Mitchell Kemble wrote it, a man of past three lore halls of the main land. This fresh form was set right by Walter de Gray Birch, a chief hand of the writ room of the great store house of the realm. It came out at London in eighteen seventy-six.

The book is writ with leave to the queen of that age, as a past of the rules that gave her realm its top place past the lands of the west. Its front note says the pages give a count of the rules past which the free and state life of our fore folk of that stock was built. Those rules are shown in the frames in which they stood most clear, Kemble says.
61331-the-saxons-in-england-volume-2-of-:
John Mitchell Kemble wrote The Saxons in England as a history of the English commonwealth till the Norman Conquest. Walter de Gray Birch revised this new edition for Bernard Quaritch at London in 1876. The contents here give book two, on the principles and progress of change in England. Growth of the kingly power opens the argument in full.

Chapters treat the rights of royalty, the king's court and household, and the ealdorman. The gerefa, the witena gemot, towns, bishops, clergy, and the poor follow in order. Appendices add the dooms of London, tithe, towns, and church dues in detail. Kemble warns that early records are scarce and the first settlement lies in obscurity. Deep legal history rebuilt a lost England.
62265-a-first-book-in-writing-english:
A First Book in Writing English is a school textbook by Edwin Herbert Lewis, published in New York in eighteen ninety seven. Lewis taught English at Lewis Institute and at the University of Chicago. Chapters move from the art of writing to reading aloud and spelling. A review of punctuation and a study of grammar phases follow in order.

Later chapters teach how to divide a paragraph into sentences and how to build well knit sentences. The plan is practical, aimed at students who must write clear prose for class and for work. Lewis treats style as a craft of choices that can be learned. The book shows how composition was taught when the modern English course was still young.
62425-the-ruins-of-the-roman-city-of-uri:
The Ruins of the Roman City of Uriconium is a guide to a broke town of Rome in England by Thomas Wright. The host text is made from the fourth form of the book, of eighteen sixty three. It was put out at a shire town and at London. Cuts stand in the book. Its first words set out its aim in plain words. That aim is to give the kind of lore the crowd of guests at the dig want.

Those guests have no guide to tell what they see, those words say. They have not the fine lore of old things that would let them grasp all with no such guide. It is the first chance in this land, the words go on, to go deep in a town of past four teen ages.
62999-wit-character-folklore-customs-of-:
Richard Blakeborough wrote Wit, Character, Folklore and Customs of the North Riding of Yorkshire. The book adds a glossary of over four thousand words and idioms now in use. Henry Frowde issued it at London in 1898. Blakeborough was a society humorist and late honorary curator of a learned body. He had writ comedies named Tomboy and Auntie. The book is given to friends at York and Durham.

Seven chapters fill the part shown here. Four chapters in a row treat Yorkshire stories of wit and character. Customs of the year and folklore follow at chapter six. Customs of courtship, marriage, and birth open chapter seven. A long subscriber list sits at the back in this digital text. Footnotes are gathered at the end of the book, a note says. Dialect tales, seasonal rites, and a vast word list make the volume a storehouse of North Riding life.
63000-the-boy-in-the-bush:
The Boy in the Bush is a novel by Lawrence and Skinner, published by Thomas Seltzer in New York in 1924. Its hero, Jack, steps ashore at Fremantle in West Australia looking, as the narrator says, like a lamb. He is a good-looking boy with a London saddle in his kit and a letter of introduction in his pocket. England has sent him out, and the bush will test what the lamb look hides.

The chapters follow him to Wandoo station: driving in, the twin lambs, and yard work. Christmas and New Year's Eve pass, along with blows, a ride with Tom, and gold. An offer to Mary and a last ride under the sign of the rider on the red horse close the book. Its outback is both a place of work and a proving ground for a boy's freedom.
63020-madrid-an-historical-description-a:
Madrid is a handbook to the Spanish capital by Albert Calvert, printed at London and New York in 1909. It stands in the Spanish Series, which Calvert edited, with volumes on Toledo, Seville, and the Prado. His title promises an historical description and handbook. Four hundred fifty-three pictures fill its pages.

Ten chapters run from first impressions of the city to the café life of the Madrileños. Calvert treats the city's history, its court and society, and its art. Churches and public buildings get a chapter, and Alcalá de Henares gets one too. Two chapters go to the bull-fight and the bull-fighter's art. The book packs a whole capital between covers.
63400-these-are-the-british:
These Are the British, by Drew Middleton, was published in New York in 1957. Middleton says close ties since 1940 left many Americans still ignorant of modern Britain. He offers a picture of the country, warts and all. He warns that the book is uneven by need. Some sides of British life, such as religion, are left untouched.

He stresses sides least known in the United States. Ascot, he grants, is showy but tells little about modern Britain. He wants readers to see what changed since 1945. The society he shows is modern and mobile, strong in body and mind. The foreword ends with Franklin's old warning that friends must hang together or hang apart.
64310-fairy-tales-told-in-the-bush:
Fairy Tales Told in the Bush holds tales for the young by Sister Agnes. A front print shows a room whose walls are all shelves of books. The book came out in London, and no year is shown in its front pages. Tales blend home lore with the lore of the Australian bush.

A boy who lied leads, then a magic gun and a stream dug deep in earth. The birth tale of a great river of that land earns its own part. A lost scent flower, a house of truth, and wild beasts fill the set. Prints show honey theft, moon trips, and toys that run off at night. Soft morals tune the tales for school and home in a new land.
64319-the-history-of-esculent-fish:
The History of Esculent Fish treats food fish, with plates drawn and cut by Eleazar Albin. An essay on breeding fish and building fish ponds, by Roger North, joins it. The London printing is dated seventeen ninety four and sold for a guinea and a half. Elizabeth Albin drew the barbel plate in seventeen thirty six.

The barbel opens the accounts, named for the beard under its chaps or nose. It is a middling table fish, best angled from May to August at dawn or dusk. Salmon spawn, lob worms, and old cheese steeped in honey serve as its baits. The carp follows, called the most prized fish for stocking ponds in England. Marchal first brought it to England about fifteen fourteen, the text says. Prussian and Bohemian nobles draw great revenue from carp pond sales.
64432-anguish-languish:
Anguish Languish is a comic book on sound alike words by Howard Chace, printed in nineteen fifty six. Prentice Hall published it at Englewood Cliffs, with a society for the languish behind it. That society's slogan is Anguish for Everybody, and it backs the little text. Four parts hold rewritten tales, rhymes, and songs in the new tongue.

The trick is to swap each English word for others that sound the same. Little Red Riding Hood becomes Ladle Rat Rotten Hut in Chace's rendering. Mary Had a Little Lamb turns into Marry Hatter Ladle Limb in the set. A mock professor of Anguish complains that boys and girls sound like poisoned gulls. Cups and saucers, he shows, pass for cops and sorcerers in careless ears. The book argues that the setting, not the sound, tells us what words mean.
64471-the-book-of-light-in-the-hand-of-l:
Vaughan, master of the Temple and chaplain in ordinary to the Queen, preached a sermon in St Paul's Cathedral on Tuesday, April 30, 1872. It was a plea for the British and Foreign Bible Society, and he published it by request at London the same year. His texts are two sayings of John: God is Light, and God is Love.

Round these two centres, he says, revolves the theology of St John: not Calvinism, not Arminianism, not Romanism, not Protestantism, but two principles higher and deeper than any question dividing parties. God is the light of truth, of holiness, of direction, and of comfort, he begins. A cathedral sermon turned charity appeal for the Bible's circulation is the pamphlet.
65384-and-five-were-foolish:
Dornford Yates published this set of tales with Ward, Lock and Company in London and Melbourne. Yates dedicates the book to Richard, whose worst fault, he jokes, is that he is growing up. Five long stories fill the contents, each named for a woman or a season.

Sarah opens the book, followed by Madeleine and then Katharine in turn. Spring comes fourth, and Elizabeth closes the set at the end. Yates was known for polished tales of love, money and manners among the well-off. A biblical echo in the title, of wise and foolish attendants, hangs over these stories of choice and chance.
65674-the-adventures-of-a-marmotte-sold-:
The Adventures of a Marmotte is a children's tale written to raise money for the distressed Irish, published in London by Simpkin and Marshall in 1831. Eliza Grey signs the preface in June of that year. The little book sold at one shilling, and its whole price was charity.

Grey asks readers to forgive its faults for the sake of its cause. Then the marmot tells its own history, a boldness it confesses at once. Its first memory is of lying curled like a little ball with its brothers and sisters. The animal writes, it says, to amuse children and procure a few shillings for the poor starving Irish. Famine relief in 1831 drew on such small generosities. A talking marmot in a shilling pamphlet is philanthropy at its most Victorian and most charming.
65856-cincinnati-s-old-cunny-a-notorious:
Cincinnati's Old Cunny, a short history pamphlet by Linden Edwards, was prepared by the staff of the Public Library of Fort Wayne and Allen County in 1955. The pamphlet belongs to a local history series issued under the library boards. Its title names its subject at once: a Cincinnati man known as Old Cunny, famed as a trader in human flesh.

A front sketch gives Edwards' own path, from his birth in Lewisville, Ohio, in 1899 to degrees at Ohio State and posts teaching anatomy. That medical training fits the grim theme, since tales of body trade in the Ohio Valley touch doctors, schools, and graves. The pamphlet preserves a dark scrap of river-city lore in short, factual form.
65997-the-land-of-fetish:
Ellis, a chief of the First West India corps, wrote on fetish lands of Africa. His book came out in London in 1883. He wrote West African Sketches in his past road works. The Gambia and Bathurst lead his list of coast parts. Jolloffs, odd ads, and a left road fill its first page list.

St James Island and grave ways end that first long part. British Combo and a small bill make gay talk in part two. Odd chiefs of towns and the Gambia guard stand in that list. A new field for sport men is hailed in its bold close. The Slave Coast and Whydah start the grave third part. Faith and rule mix.
6656-the-kiltartan-poetry-book-prose-tra:
Lady Gregory turns Irish poems into plain prose in The Kiltartan Poetry Book, drawing on songs she knew from childhood. She recalls Moore's melodies sung at a piano, a governess vexed by talk of Malachi's collar of gold, and later ballads nearer to the country's own tradition than Moore's faint sentiment. Love of country, she says, grew with those songs.

The translations keep the tales and feeling of the Irish originals, without forcing them into English rhyme. Readers meet heroes, lovers, and old griefs in a voice that feels close to the hearth. The Kiltartan Poetry Book is a gentle, valuable bridge from Irish song to English readers.
67503-parts-of-speech-essays-on-english:
Brander Matthews wrote Parts of Speech, essays on English, for Scribner at New York in 1901. Matthews taught in Columbia University, and gives the book to his colleague Carpenter. The essays were written across ten years, yet share one aim, he says. That aim is to make plain that English belongs to the peoples who speak it. It is their own prized possession, to deal with at their pleasure and at their peril.

That fact should be obvious, Matthews holds, yet it is not taken up on all sides. So he draws out what the fact implies, essay by essay. His stance is that of the man of letters, not the dry grammarian. A wise critic cited here calls spelling like society, never quite still or whole. Readers get lively essays on how English lives, grows, and resists its keepers.
68613-how-to-write-the-history-of-a-pari:
A handbook of local history by J Charles Cox, published at London in 1879. Bemrose and Sons issued it from London and Derby. Cox had written notes on Derbyshire's churches. Clergy in the Lincoln diocese prompted this booklet. A projected Lincolnshire county history needed parish histories first. His Derbyshire introduction was too local to reuse, he felt.

The handbook therefore generalises the method for any county. Manorial and ecclesiastical history both fall within its scope. Cox draws on Thomas's handbook to the public records. Sims's manual for topographers and genealogists helps further. He discusses only documents he knows personally, he promises. Bibliographies point beginners to the best topographical literature. The little book helped launch England's parish history industry.
69236-the-high-school-course-in-english:
Willard Bleyer, a teacher of English at Wisconsin, set out a high school course in English in a form dated 1907. Parts treat the aim of the course, its plan, and how class groups and teacher talks should run. Theme craft gets long care, from how to write and mark themes to how to file and talk through them.

Reading holds the next chief place, with notes on choice of books and use of the school shelf. Year by year plans run from first year word craft to fourth year tales, plays, songs, and essays. A list of set reads for four years and a full shelf list of aids close the guide.
70030-off-the-bluebush:
Off the Bluebush is a book of verses by John Philip Bourke, an Australian poet who wrote as Bluebush. The book is dedicated to the West and the people of the West. Western Australia is hailed as the golden state of golden hearts. A poem at the front asks that no white roses be brought when he is dead. Red roses, full blown and sun-kissed, are the ones his life missed. An editor's note tells of the poet's mates and of the young artist Ned Wethered, who drew the pictures.

The contents list songs of the goldfields life. Stamps, creeks, and flats give the pieces their names: Bummer's Creek, Pennyweight Flat. Songs of parting and of mates make the other strain. Bourke wrote for the mining towns of the west, of which he was one. The book is a rough, warm store of bush verse.
70279-bertha-weisser-s-wish:
A Christmas story by an author signing only initials, published at Boston in 1865. Bertha Weisser lives in a back attic in one of the meanest streets of the great city, with four merry little siblings steaming their damp clothes by the stove.

On a dreary October evening Bertha stares past the crowded court, thinking hard on something that fills her whole mind. The contents promise her wish, little Mary's home, Tim turning policeman, and Berty running away for the last time. Later chapters bring a hospital, Mrs Grey's suspicion, and the wish fulfilled at a chapel service. The book opens with a litany line: Lord, write all thy laws in our hearts. Children get a Christmas tale of poverty and kindness.
70444-french-english:
Philip Gilbert Hamerton compared the French and English peoples of his age in a book printed in London and New York in 1889. Seven pieces in the Atlantic Monthly in 1886 and 1887 grew into the book, much rewritten and enlarged. Hamerton had written The Intellectual Life. He says his work is not history, but a comparison of the two nations in the late nineteenth century.

Parts deal with education, patriotism, politics, and religion. In England, he finds, formal physical training is scant, and the English do not love gymnastic exercise as a science. French and English views of liberty, stability, and national pride are weighed side by side. The book serves readers who knew both lands from travel.
7065-children-of-the-bush:
Henry Lawson gathers Children of the Bush, opening with Send Round the Hat and its creed from the Book of the Bush. If a man is in a hole, the verse says, pass round the hat, were he jail bird or gentleman once. Contents add That Pretty Girl in the Army, Lord Douglas, the blindness of One Eyed Bogan, two sundowners, and a sketch of mateship on the tucker track.

A bush publican's lament, the shearer's dream, and the lost souls hotel follow. The boozers home, the romance of the swag, a bush fire, a house never built, and a droving yarn come after. Getting back on Dave Regan, His Brother's Keeper, and the ghosts of many Christmases close the set. Lawson writes Australian bush life in yarns of mateship, drink, and hard luck.
71313-the-last-crash:
The Last Crash is an aviation story by Kenneth Latour, author of The Sky Call. An editor's note singles the story out. Most aviation tales, he says, are good stories with aviation in them, but this one is a real air story by a man who knows the trade and its spirit.

The hero is John Norris, remembered for the first straight flight from Langstrom Field to Cristobal. Norris had a touch of the mystic in him, the narrator says, as most airmen do. Unlike most, he spoke his ideas aloud. His conviction was that things do not happen but are arranged. The story tests that fatalism in the air. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
71505-through-india-and-burmah-with-pen-:
Through India and Burmah with Pen and Brush is a roam book by Hugh Fisher. A Laurie house of London brought it out in its day in full. The Moat at Fort Dufferin in Mandalay stands as front plate here. Part names open at Rangoon and climb the Irrawaddy to Bhamo. A Shan chief meet and the dead heart of a realm fill first ranks.

Mandalay, south India shrine lands, and Calcutta fill next part names. First sight of the great snow range and Benares stand mid scheme. Lucknow, Cawnpore, the house of dream, and Delhi fill more ranks. Shoe guard, gate of realm, Punjab chief town, and Nabha court stand late. Rajputana, Sir Pratap Singh, and the Moharam feast close the scheme.
71788-the-house-on-the-marsh:
Florence Warden published The House on the Marsh, a romance, at New York in 1884. Thirty chapters carry the tale. The narrator tells her own story: at eighteen she cut out an advertisement headed Wanted, a Governess; must be young, and answered it eagerly, since her youth had blocked every other engagement.

She sent her photograph and qualifications, and within a week was travelling down to Geldham in Norfolk. Her charge is one little girl aged six, at thirty-five pounds a year. The child's father carried on the correspondence and promised to meet her at the market town station. Readers get a governess novel of the marsh country, opening in hope.
7179-beside-the-bonnie-brier-bush:
Ian Maclaren gathers tales of a Scottish parish called Drumtochty. A schoolmaster, a Highland mystic, a wise woman, and an old-school doctor share one small world there. Domsie, the lad of parts, carries the news to Whinnie Knowe, a scholar gets a funeral, and Lachlan Campbell passes through bitter shame toward a child's trust. Each sketch stands alone, yet all belong to the same glen.

Maclaren writes with warmth for plain folk, letting sermons, gardens, floods, and sickbeds show character better than fine speeches. The brier bush of the title marks a home ground, modest and well loved, and the book's charm lies in its close watch of village talk and feeling. It reads like a visit to neighbours long remembered.
72013-lefty-o-the-bush:
Burt Standish's baseball story, copyrighted in 1914 and published by Grosset and Dunlap in New York, follows his earlier Lefty books into the bush leagues. The frontispiece shows the slide that names the hero: spikes first, Locke slid.

Forty-six chapters carry the season, from Out in the Bush and The Man to Pitch through A Pitchers' Battle and The Squeeze Play to The Forgery and Cleared Up. The first chapter finds Mike Riley, manager of the Bancroft Bullies, studying the Kingsbridge batting order on the opening Saturday. The Northern League is a genuine bush organization, and this is the first game of the season at Kingsbridge, a crude, hustling pulp-mill town. The grand stand fills fast as the mills close at three.
73017-pomona-or-the-future-of-english:
Basil de Sélincourt asks what comes next for the tongue in Pomona, or The Future of English. Dutton of New York holds the copyright of 1928. The first page turns the theme round: in these swift science days, has language itself a future at all?

He quotes Haldane and his essay Daedalus. Two folk on earth may soon be present to each other in a flash of time, Haldane wrote. Will speech keep a place at such speed, Sélincourt asks. Folk may not need to speak at all, in German, Japanese, or Esperanto. The essay then weighs that bright, strange fear for the mother tongue.
73379-in-the-brush:
In the Brush recalls old-time life in the American Southwest. Pierson wrote the sketches from his own ministry. Appleton published the book in New York in 1881. Pierson had presided over Cumberland College in Kentucky. Sheppard drew the illustrations. Sixteen chapters gather his experiences.

The first chapter explains his purpose. A friend in New York once asked him a plain question. Did anything strange or funny ever happen to a missionary? She had read the missionary papers since childhood. Pierson kept her question for thirty years. His chapters answer it with stories. Basket-meetings and barbecue weddings appear. A Scotch baby is baptised in the wilds. Circuit-riders and illiterate preachers fill later pages.
73560-the-cult-of-the-chafing-dish:
The Cult of the Chafing Dish, by Frank Schloesser, came out in London. Gay and Bird published it in May 1904; a second edition followed in 1905. A passage from Ruskin on cookery heads the book. Cookery, for Ruskin, means knowing herbs, fruits, balms, and spices. Schloesser gives his book to the only woman who could turn him from bachelordom. Ten chapters follow: soups, fish, flesh and fowl, salads, eggs, sauces, and sweets. Chapter one sings the dish itself. Every bachelor, Schloesser writes, has a wife of some sort. His is a chafing dish, nicknamed Chaffinda. She is nickel-plated, on a wrought-iron stand, with a spirit lamp.

He bought her at Harrod's for twelve shillings and ninepence. The book addresses bachelors in chambers, young couples, and yachtsmen. A quick, hot, light meal is its whole gospel.
73604-the-red-fetish:
Frank Belknap Long wrote a weird tale that ran in Weird Tales in January 1930. A picture shows men writhing in the sun like wounded snakes. Bill Cullen shades his eyes and stares at an empty skyline on a beach. His arms show scraggy and thin, his features pinched and black. Strong winds and enormous seas have beaten the shore and deepened his helplessness.

Look here, he tells his companion, it is physically impossible to hang on without water, so what do you say to a swim. Wellington Van Wyck, a frightened little man with pointed fox like ears, groans and shakes his head. Folk call him a coward. Thirst, fear, and a red fetish drive the castaway tale.
74183-my-heart-and-my-flesh:
Elizabeth Madox Roberts wrote a novel printed at New York in 1927, with a second printing before the book was even out. Roberts had earlier written a novel called The Time of Man and a book of poems. A line from the Psalms, on heart and flesh crying out for the living God, gives the book its title.

A prologue follows a child named Luce running to a store for lamp oil as dark falls. A lamp lighter climbs his ladder across the street, as he does each day at the same step. Luce thinks of Mome, a city of electric light, where the richest man in the world keeps his money house.
75439-the-king-s-english:
The King English is a tongue craft book by the Fowler brothers, Henry and Francis. A Clarendon press brought out this second print in nineteen twenty four. Both men made the Concise Oxford word book of their day in past work. Part one of the scheme treats word stock in its first rank. Plain and far sought words, short and long words, head its rules there.

Word slips, new coin words, home land words, and slang fill that part. Part two treats clause craft, case, count, and kin word choice in rank. Shall and will get a long rule run in that part of the book. Part three treats airs and graces, wit kinds, trim word shift, and old forms. Trope, repeat, and trim speech close the scheme of the whole book.
77263-the-history-of-a-pot-of-varnish:
The History of a Pot of Varnish is an essay taken from Scribner's Monthly, published by Murphy and Company, varnish makers, and copyrighted in 1880 at Newark and Cleveland. It opens on the American love of the practical in the industrial arts. With that love, it says, Americans join a ready gift for finding an interest near romance in the origin and making of useful, plain things.

Everybody knows something, the essay goes on, about the bright, amber-colored fluid called varnish. Few know how varied and interesting a story is wrapped up in it. Varnish factories are few, and their doors seldom stand wide open. The fluid speaks to the nose of its close companionship with turpentine. Its sticky quality and elastic body come from a third ingredient, the resinous juice of a tree.
77335-poems-scots-and-english:
John Buchan wrote these poems, Scots and English, printed at London and Edinburgh in 1917. A list of his other books at the front names his romances, from Prester John and The Thirty-Nine Steps to Greenmantle. Buchan dedicates the verses to his brother Alastair, a lieutenant in the Royal Scots Fusiliers who fell at Arras on Easter Monday 1917.

A note on the Scots pieces says they use the speech of the Lowland hill country, from the Cheviots to Galloway. Buchan could speak that tongue, he says, more easily than he could write it. Book one holds the Scots poems: Midian's Evil Day, The Herd of Farawa, and The Eternal Feminine. A Shorter Catechism piece and Theocritus turned into Scots follow, then war poems under the head Inter Arma.
77838-an-essay-on-hasheesh:
Victor Robinson's An Essay on Hasheesh, printed in New York in 1912 by the Medical Review of Reviews, gathers his observations and experiments with the drug. Robinson was a pharmaceutical chemist at Columbia University and a member of the American Chemical Society, and he had already written Pathfinders in Medicine.

The opening pages argue that ailing man has ransacked the world for balms against pain, since the smallest inflamed nerve can bend the proudest spirit. Quoted voices frame the inquiry, from John Addington Symonds, who named hasheesh the modern man's remaining refuge, to the hemp-field scents in Allen's Reign of Law. Even Caesar, he notes, lost the lustre of his eye to a fever.
7815-hereward-the-last-of-the-english:
Hereward the Last of the English retells the outlaw hero's life in chapter titles that read like a saga roll. Outlawed, he seeks fortune north, slays a bear, rescues a Cornish princess twice, serves Ranald of Waterford, wrecks on Flanders shore, and fights at Guisnes.

Later he wins magic armor, is taken for a magician, turns berserk, wins the mare Swallow, rides into Bruges as a beggar, and clears Bourne of Frenchmen. Made knight in English fashion, he faces Ivo Taillebois and Norman rule. The book keeps an old English hero alive in plain, stirring prose.
79518-flesh:
Karl W Detzer wrote Flesh, a tale of a Chicago fireman and his horses. Paddy Maguire was born on the tailboard, as firemen say of their own. His father Ham led a hose company by the South Water Street docks. The Great Fire of eighteen hundred seventy one took the old man.

Paddy was ten when the bells rang that warm October day. He saw his father charge the flames at dawn and fall by dusk. General Sheridan blew up houses with powder to stop the fire. At seventeen Paddy joined Engine Ten and served forty years. Reels, steam, and horse teams gave the work its hard romance. He drove chiefs’ buggies and great three horse hitches in his prime. Made lieutenant in nineteen hundred seven, he scorned the new motor wagons. Gasoline can not be trusted in fire work, he swore to the end.
8132-life-in-the-clearings-versus-the-bu:
Susanna Moodie, author of Roughing It in the Bush, wrote this sequel about life in the clearings, the settled towns of Upper Canada, as against the bush. Dedicated to her husband John Wedderburn Dunbar Moodie, sheriff of Hastings County, it sketches Belleville, local improvements, free schools. Amusements, camp meetings, mourning customs, odd characters, and trials of a travelling musician and a singing master. Her motto claims she sketches from nature, and the draught is true.

Moodie writes from painful experience in a distant land, now with the confidence of a settler rather than a newcomer. The book gives a lively social history of Canadian town life in the mid-nineteenth century. For readers of pioneer literature, it is the essential companion to her bush classic, showing what came after the clearing.
8888-the-wept-of-wish-ton-wish:
James Fenimore Cooper writes The Wept of Wish-Ton-Wish as a tale of early New England. Opening with Rogers's lines on a girl dead to him and to all, her lute silent, her fairy step heard no more on stairs or at the door. The 1871 edition dedicates the book to a Pennsylvania clergyman who furnished its materials, thanked publicly as far as his reluctance to appear allows. Cooper notes that many families share striking early histories, and his tale draws on one such family's past.

The story follows a Puritan household on the Connecticut frontier, its children carried off by Native people, and the long aftermath of captivity, return, and divided loyalties. Cooper's treatment of Native characters and of Puritan rigidity reflects his time and invites critical reading today.
9987-stories-by-foreign-authors-spanish:
This 1898 collection gathers five Spanish stories in English translation, chosen to show Spain's storytellers to American readers. Pedro Antonio de Alarcón contributes The Tall Woman, a ghost tale, and Moors and Christians, while José Selgas offers The White Butterfly.

Gustavo Adolfo Bécquer's The Organist and Fernán Caballero's Bread Cast Upon the Waters complete the set, moving from the uncanny to village kindness and everyday faith. The stories are short, polished, and varied in mood. Readers get a compact introduction to nineteenth-century Spanish fiction, from haunted rooms to country roads.
a-jolly-by-josh: This unknown jolly by Josh opens aboard a Lake Shore Limited train crossing the continent. The narrator, seeking a way to pass time, studies fellow travelers and finds them uniformly uninteresting. His mind wanders out the window to the advance of civilization beside the track. The sketch promises a humorous traveler's tale.
a-pocket-dictionary-welsh-english: William Richards compiles this pocket dictionary of Welsh and English, revised, corrected, and enlarged for travellers and learners. Its Welsh preface notes a growing desire among Welsh speakers to know English better, matched by English visitors making real efforts to learn Welsh in the summer months. Against bulkier works stuffed with words never used, the volume aims at a practical word list for everyday mastery of a foreign tongue.
a-tale-of-a-lonely-parish: Francis Marion Crawford tells a tale of a lonely parish, dedicated to his mother from Sorrento on Christmas Day 1885. The Reverend Augustin Ambrose, growing old with failing sight, would gladly give up taking pupils. He is weary of Thucydides, Homer, Todhunter, conic sections, and even his beloved Horace. He faces dull young men who cannot keep up and clever ones unprepared for an English university, drilling the first by repetition and memoria technica.
beside-the-bonnie-brier-bush:
Ian Maclaren's Beside the Bonnie Brier Bush gathers Scottish parish sketches centred on the village of Drumtochty. Maclaren's contents include Domsie the schoolmaster, a Highland mystic, a mother's sermon, the transformation of Lachlan Campbell, and a doctor of the old school.

The Revolution has reached the parish, Maclaren notes, bringing a School Board with chairman, clerk, treasurer and officer. Yet the glen's life goes on: sermons tasted, floods crossed, deaths fought and mourned. Maclaren writes with affectionate humour and deep feeling for Scottish rural character. Readers who love Scots village life will find these sketches tender, funny and enduring.
books-and-characters-french-english:
Lytton Strachey published Books and Characters, French and English, first in London in May 1922, and dedicated the set to John Maynard Keynes. Strachey gathers essays that had run in the Independent Review, the New Quarterly, the Athenaeum, and the Edinburgh Review. One Voltaire dialogue prints here for the first time.

Racine opens the set, and Sir Thomas Browne and Shakespeare's final period follow. Voltaire takes the center ground: his time in England, his tragedies, and his dealings with Frederick the Great. The Rousseau affair, Blake's poetry, and Henri Beyle get sharp short studies. Lady Hester Stanhope and Mr Creevey close the cast. Strachey's cool, witty prose made the set a model of the modern literary essay.
britannica-1911-balkash:
Balkash, or Balkhash, is a great lake of Asiatic Russia in the Kirghiz steppes. It lies between the governments of Semipalatinsk and Semiryechensk, about 600 miles east of Lake Aral. The 1911 Britannica entry ranks it fourth among the lakes of Eurasia, with an area of 7,115 square miles at 900 feet above the sea.

Shaped like a broad crescent some 430 miles long, the lake has a bleak plateau, the Famine Steppe, on its north-west shore and low ground to the south-east. The Ili river is its chief feeder, joined by the Karatal, Aksu, Lepsa, and Ayaguz. Though it has no outlet, its water stays fairly fresh, and it freezes from about November to April.
britannica-1911-bangash:
The Bangash are a small tribe of Pathans in the Kohat district of India's North-West Frontier Province. They hold the hills between Thal and Kohat, and they number some 3,000 fighting men. The 1911 Britannica entry is a brief one, built on their moves across that hill country.

Long ago the Bangash owned the whole of Kurram. Pressed by the Turis, they shifted east, drove out the Orakzais, and took their land in the Kohat district, west of the Khattak country. A closing note rates the physique of both Bangash and Khattaks as exceptionally good and calls them excellent soldiers.
britannica-1911-bentinck-lord-william-ge:
Lord William George Frederick Cavendish Bentinck, better known as Lord George Bentinck (1802–1848), was a British politician. Second surviving son of the fourth duke of Portland, he was schooled at home and took a cornet’s commission in the 10th Hussars at seventeen. He left the army in 1822 and served his uncle George Canning as private secretary.

From 1828 Bentinck sat for Lynn-Regis, his uncle’s old seat, for the rest of his life. Weak speaking kept him obscure in parliament, while on the turf his honesty and drive made him a leader. Only in his last three years did those gifts turn to politics, where he rose fast as a Protection champion before dying suddenly at Welbeck in 1848.
britannica-1911-brush:
Brush, from the French brosse, is an instrument for removing dust and dirt from surfaces, or for laying on paint and whitewash. It is made of a tuft or tufts of fibrous or flexible material fixed to a solid stock. The word also means the undergrowth of a wood in both French and English. Whether both senses share one root, a bundle of brushwood used as a broom, is historically doubtful.

Materials for brush making run wide: feathers, pig's bristles, the hair of certain animals, whalebone, rubber, split cane, broom-corn and coir all serve. Brushes of birch twigs with long handles are often called brooms, a term also used for household dust brushes but not for paint brushes. Two kinds divide the trade: simple brushes of one tuft, such as hair pencils and painters' tools.
britannica-1911-calash: A calash is a light carriage with a hood that folds down. The word comes from the French caleche, drawn from a Polish word for a wheeled carriage. The Canadian calash has two wheels. Its driver sits on a seat set on the splash-board at the front. The word also names a kind of hood once worn by women. That hood was made of silk stretched over hoops to hold its shape.
britannica-1911-cash:
Cash is the subject of a word and trade article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word first meant a box where money is kept, from a French word for a case. It now means ready money or coin. In banking use it can mean coin alone. It can also cover bank notes, as against bills or drafts. To cash a cheque means to turn it into coin.

The article then treats the cash on delivery system in detail. A tradesman sends goods through a carrier agency. The carrier collects the sum due on delivery, or sends the goods back if no money is paid. Express firms run the system in America, and post offices run it in much of Europe. It does away with credit and with paying in advance. The text links the rise of large catalogue houses in America to this system.
britannica-1911-cat-fish:
Cat-fish is an animal article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about the fishes of the family Siluridae. The name comes from the long barbels or feelers about the mouth, which men have likened to the whiskers of a cat. The group is large and varied and lives mostly in fresh water. Some kinds, strange in shape and armour, recall the mailed fishes of the Devonian age. Agassiz once placed them near those fossils, but later science sets them beside the carps in the group Ostariophysi.

Between them the true cat-fishes count over a thousand species spread through the fresh waters of the world, thickest between the tropics and missing from western Europe. The kind that gives the family its name is the Wels, Silurus glanis, the largest fresh water fish of Europe, with a broad head, a wide mouth, and six barbels.
britannica-1911-cornbrash:
Cornbrash, a band of rock in England, is explained in a geology entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is the top member of the Bathonian stage of the Jurassic set. The name is an old farm term from Wiltshire for loose rubble that makes good corn soil. William Smith took it up for a thin band of shelly limestone.

Thin as it is, at ten to twenty five feet, the band runs a long way. It can be traced from Weymouth to the Yorkshire coast. In north Lincolnshire it thins to near nothing, then shows again in bays farther north. The rock is rich in fossils that mark a shift between two great sets. Named shell kinds and a large ammonite lead the list. Remains of sea reptiles turn up at times as well. The stone serves for local building, though it has little worth for roads.
britannica-1911-crash:
Crash is a trade term in cloth work for a kind of narrow towel, from fourteen to twenty inches wide, as a short 1911 Britannica article explains. The name is probably of Russian origin. The simplest, coarsest type is known as Russia crash, made from grey flax or tow yarns.

Other kinds are classed as grey, boiled, bleached, plain, twilled, and fancy crash, with many sorts of border. In later years cotton came into use for the warp, and mixed and jute yarns for the weft. When finished, the cloth is cut into lengths of about three yards, the two ends sewn together, and hung over a roller. From that use comes its other name, roller towelling.
britannica-1911-crayfish:
Crayfish are freshwater crustaceans that are close kin to lobsters and, like them, belong to the order Macrura. Two families divide the group by hemisphere. The Astacidae live in northern waters, and the Parastacidae live in southern waters. The common kind in England and Ireland is about three or four inches long. It has a dull green or brown back and a paler underside.

These animals shelter under stones or in burrows dug in river banks and come out at night to feed. They eat insects, snails, frogs, and carrion, and some are said to come on land for plant food. The entry traces their range across Europe, Asia, and North America, noting blind kinds in caves such as Mammoth Cave in Kentucky. Southern kinds occur in Australia, New Zealand, Madagascar, and South America, and some large ones serve as food.
britannica-1911-cuttle-fish:
Cuttle-fish is a common name for the better known kinds of the mollusc class Cephalopoda. Squid, octopus, and nautilus are their kin in that class. The name cuttle-fish fits above all the common Sepia. Sepia is marked by an inner shell of lime, known as cuttle-bone. It also has an ink sac, whose contents have long been used as a pigment called sepia.

The name squid is used by fishermen for the ten-armed kinds whose shell is a soft, unlimed piece like a pen. In Italian a squid is called by a word for a reed pen, and the English term calamary is at times used in the same way. Like Sepia, squids have the ink sac. That shared trait has earned them the name pen and ink fish. In German both groups are called ink fishes.
britannica-1911-flat-fish:
Flat-fish, family Pleuronectidae, is the common name for fishes that swim on their side, such as the halibut, turbot, brill, plaice, flounder and sole. The side turned to the bottom, right in some kinds and left in others, is usually colourless. It is called blind, since it bears no eye. The upper side, turned to the light, carries both eyes and is often coloured, in some tropical kinds vividly. Bones and muscles of the upper side are the stronger.

Yet flat-fish hatch symmetrical, like other fishes, and only later take their twisted form. The entry weighs which group of bony fishes their ancestors were, rejecting the old idea that they are merely modified codfish. It follows their structure, their kinds and their spread. About 500 species are known, mostly marine, with a few sole-like kinds in fresh water.
britannica-1911-flatbush:
Flatbush was formerly a township of Kings county, Long Island, New York. It was annexed to Brooklyn in 1894 and, from 1 January 1898, formed part of the borough of Brooklyn in New York City. Dutch settlers founded it about 1651 and called it Midwout, Midwoud or Medwoud, from Dutch words for middle and wood. For some twenty years that name held. Then Vlachte Bos, wooded plain, grew common, and by corruption became Flatbush.

Farming was the chief work of the early settlers on this Long Island plain. In August 1776 the village felt the American Revolutionary War at close quarters. Cornwallis's division occupied it on 23 August. Four days later, at the battle of Long Island, sometimes called the battle of Flatbush, General Sullivan's troops defended Flatbush Pass, a key point on the road. The short entry gives the place its Dutch naming story, its annexation, and that one hard-fought day.
britannica-1911-gararish: Gararish, also written Kararish, is a brief tribe note in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The Gararish are a half nomad tribe of Semitic origin living along the right bank of the Nile from Wadi Halfa to Merawi. Many of them farm the land, while others work as guides or transport drivers. They call themselves kin to the Ababda, yet the article judges them more Arab than Beja.
britannica-1911-garnish:
Garnish is the subject of a short word study in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry traces the word to Old French forms of garnir, meaning to furnish or equip. Its root links to words for warning and guarding. The first sense was thus to fit out or guard, and only later to adorn.

Inside, the entry shows how that old sense of warning lives on in law. A garnishee is a person who holds money owed to a debtor. A court warns that person not to pay the debtor, but to pay a third party instead. Cross links point to attachment, execution, and bankruptcy for more detail.
britannica-1911-globe-fish:
Globe-fish, also called sea-hedgehogs, are sea fishes known for a strange power. They can swell their stomachs full of air. They belong to two families, the Diodonts and the Tetrodonts. Their jaws look like the sharp beak of a parrot. Bone and teeth are fused into one mass with a sharp edge. With those jaws they snap off bits of coral and chew other hard food.

Most globe-fish are short, thick, and round in build, with strong fins. Thick skin with no scales covers the body. Spines of varied shape stud the skin. When the fish fills itself with air, it takes a ball shape. The spines then jut out and form a rough suit of armour. A fish blown up in this way turns over and floats belly up.
britannica-1911-goldfish:
The goldfish is a fish of the carp family, native to China. It has spread to and settled in other lands. In the wild state its hues match those of a crucian carp. Like that fish, it is hard to kill and easy to tame. White forms are quite common. In most of those pale fish the hue is a bright orange or gold.

The Chinese have kept these pale fish for a long time. By careful choice of breed stock they have raised all the odd forms seen in tame stock. In some fish the back fin is half its due length, and in some it is gone in full. In others all the fins run to near twice the usual length. The snout is often out of shape as well. At times even the gold hue is lost, and the fish is white or silver.
britannica-1911-hag-fish:
The hag-fish, also called the glutinous hag or borer, is a marine fish. Its scientific name is Myxine. With the lampreys it forms the Cyclostomata. That group is one of the lowest orders of vertebrates. The hag-fish resembles a lamprey in form. It is usually found inside dead cod or haddock. It buries itself in the abdomen and feeds on the flesh.

When caught, it secretes thick glutinous slime. It pours out so much that people believed it turned water into glue. The fish lives in the North Atlantic. Other temperate seas hold it too. Some coasts take it in large numbers. Scotland's east coast and California's west coast are named. The entry is a single tight paragraph of natural history. Note: this record's hosted file is a shared page chunk; the hag-fish entry stands complete within it.
britannica-1911-joash:
Joash, also called Jehoash, is the name of two kings in the Bible, treated together in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The name in Hebrew means that Yahweh is strong, or has given. The first Joash was a son of Ahaziah and king of Judah. He won the throne by a revolt in which Athaliah died.

His rise was sealed by a solemn pact and the sack of the temple of Baal. The priest Jehoiada ruled in fact while the king was young. Later the king bought off an attack on Jerusalem by the Aramaeans. He died by a plot whose cause is not clear. The second Joash ruled Israel and won back towns lost to Syria. His taunt of the thistle and the cedar, sent to the king of Judah, is called famed.
britannica-1911-lachish:
Lachish was a town of great importance in southern Palestine, often named in the Tell el-Amarna tablets. Joshua destroyed it for joining the league against the Gibeonites, and it was assigned to the tribe of Judah. Rehoboam fortified it. King Amaziah fled there and was murdered by conspirators. Sennacherib campaigned against it while Hezekiah tried to make terms; the campaign is pictured in bas-reliefs from Nineveh now in the British Museum. It was also one of the last cities to resist Nebuchadnezzar.

The Onomasticon puts Lachish 7 m. from Eleutheropolis on the south road. That agrees with the accepted identification, Tell el-Hesi, a large mound dug for the Palestine Exploration Fund by Petrie and Bliss in 1890–1893. The name survives in Umm Lakis, a small Roman site nearby, probably a later home of the ancient inhabitants' descendants.
britannica-1911-maccunn-hamish:
Hamish MacCunn, a Scottish composer, is noted in a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Greenock in 1868, he was a shipowner's son there. The Royal College of Music in London gave him his training. His first hit came in 1887 at the Crystal Palace in London. An overture named Land of the Mountain and Flood won that day.

From 1888 MacCunn taught at that same college for six years. His opera Jeanie Deans was staged at Edinburgh in 1894. That year he wed a daughter of the painter John Pettie. He led the Carl Rosa opera band for some years on tour. His opera Diarmid reached Covent Garden in the year 1897. Cantatas, songs, and part-songs all bear a Scots stamp in his work.
britannica-1911-marash:
Marash is the chief town of a district in the Aleppo province of the Ottoman realm, set high at the foot of a great range. It stands east of a river, and its district lies near all in that range, with a famed Armenian hill town in it. The town thrives, the 1911 Britannica entry says.

Its trade runs in Kurd rugs and fine needle work. The air is good save in the heat of summer. Of its folk, about half are Armenians who speak Turkish. Schools and churches of an American mission, a native church of the new faith, and a Jesuit house stand in the town. Its site by the mouths of three chief passes gave it weight in the first ages, as old carved stones found there prove.
britannica-1911-osh: Osh is a town in Russian Turkestan, in the tract of Ferghana, south east of the rail end at Andijan. It stands more than four thousand feet past the sea. Its count of folk in nineteen hundred was past thirty-seven thousand. The town has two parts, one for the home folk and one for the Russian folk. A good road starts here and runs up to the Pamir hills. Guns can pass on that road. Trade with China from the town is large. The entry is a short note.
britannica-1911-oshkosh:
Oshkosh is a city and the county seat of Winnebago county, Wisconsin. It stands on the west shore of Lake Winnebago, at the mouth of the Upper Fox river, some seventy-five miles north-west of Milwaukee. Its people numbered 28,284 in 1900 and 33,062 in 1910. A large share of its folk were of German birth or German parentage. Three rail lines serve the city.

River steamboats link Oshkosh with other Fox River Valley towns, with the Wisconsin river at Portage, and with the Great Lakes at Green Bay. Electric lines run to Fond du Lac, Green Bay, and Omro. The city lies on both sides of the Fox river. Six steel bridges span the river there. The city stretches back from the shore toward Lake Butte des Morts.
britannica-1911-parish:
The 1911 Britannica article on the parish explains a word that began as the name of a bishop's district. In the early church a bishop and his priests served each district. Scattered churches were visited by travelling priests. Toward the end of the fourth century bishops set resident priests over fixed districts. The word parish settled on those districts.

The article then takes up English law. A parish is the township assigned to one priest. Its tithes and dues were paid to him. The article argues that the parish grew up beside the township, not by one act of law. The two systems covered the same ground for a thousand years. Yet they stayed separate in character. The parish system in England is traced to Theodore of Tarsus.
britannica-1911-pidgin-english: Pidgin English, also written Pigeon English, is the trade jargon of the seaports of China and of the Straits Settlements in the Far East, as a 1911 Britannica entry explains. It is built from corrupted English words with some Portuguese and Malay mixed in, all following Chinese habits of speech. Foreigners and native Chinese use it as their shared means of talk in business and port life. The word pidgin itself is the Chinese corruption of the English word business.
britannica-1911-pike-fish:
Pike is a fish article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a small family of fresh water fishes. Pike swim in the rivers and lakes of Europe, north Asia, and North America. They are known by a long, flat body with small scales and a broad, flat snout.

The article stresses the great mouth, armed with strong teeth that point back. Prey that slides in cannot slip back out. Fins set far back give the fish a sharp burst of speed. One kind fills the Old World, while North America holds more, the largest in the Great Lakes. The text calls the pike the most greedy of fresh water fish. Large ones are said to seize rats and even small dogs.
britannica-1911-pilot-fish:
Known to sailors for swimming with ships and with sharks, the pilot fish is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Its Latin name is given as Naucrates ductor. It lives in all warm and near warm seas. It is common in the sea between Europe and Africa.

In summer the fish may follow a ship as far north as the south coast of England. Old writers knew the habit well. They told of a fish that showed the way to lost sailors. The entry doubts that the fish guides a shark to food on purpose. It more likely stays close for scraps of food. In that sense it lives off its large host, much like the sucking fish.
britannica-1911-radish:
Radish is a garden plant treated in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. In botany it is a fleshy-rooted annual plant, not known in a wild state. Some forms of the wild radish of the Mediterranean coasts come so near it that it may be a grown race of that stock. It is much liked as a raw salad.

Two chief forms are grown, one with a long spindle root and one with a round turnip root. The plant does well in any well-worked soil that is not too heavy, but it wants a warm, snug spot. Seed is sown spread out in beds four or five feet wide. The beds are netted to guard them from birds. The first sowing can be made in mid December under litter, for use at the start of March.
britannica-1911-rawmarsh:
Rawmarsh is a town article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a district in the West Riding of Yorkshire, England. It stands on a ridge above the valley of the Don, north-east of Sheffield. Its people grew from 11,983 in 1891 to 14,587 in 1901. The article presents a working town built on iron and coal.

Its church of Saint Lawrence was rebuilt in 1839, save for its Norman tower. The town has large iron works, steel rolling mills, and potteries. Coal pits work in the area round it. At the Conquest the manor was granted to Walter d'Eyncourt. In the twelfth century it was split among the three daughters of his tenant Ralph Paganel. Paganel is thought to have founded the church. The entry joins an industrial present to a Norman past in a few lines.
britannica-1911-shamash:
Shamash is a myth entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It explains the sun god of Babylon and Assyria in the ancient east. His name may mean a servant, which hints at a lower rank in old times. Stone texts call him the offspring of the moon god.

The entry names his two chief shrines and their bright house title. Temples to him stood in all the great towns of the land. His chief trait is justice, since the sun brings hidden wrong to light. A famed law giver said the god moved him to gather the laws. Hymns to the god rank among the best verse of that world.
britannica-1911-starfish:
Starfish, a common name for a large set of sea animals, are covered in a 1911 Britannica article. All of them belong to the echinoderm group. They fall into three sets: the asterids, the ophiuroids, and the crinoids. The asterids are the true starfish, such as the cross fish and sun star.

The common cross fish of British seas serves as the type form. It has a central disk with five arms or rays. Its top skin is tough and laced with small lime plates and prickles. The mouth sits at the center of the underside. Grooves run from the mouth to each arm tip, with tube feet set in rows.
britannica-1911-sunfish:
Sunfish is the name of a strange sea fish found in most oceans. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica describes its odd shape and habits. Only two kinds were then known to science. The rough kind swims in all temperate and tropic seas.

The fish looks as if it has no tail at all. Its rear end is cut short to a few small bones. Tall fins above and below do the swimming work. The head merges into the trunk with no clear break. A small mouth bears a hard plate in place of teeth. In calm bright weather it rests at the top of the sea. Its high fin then shows above the water in the sun. Most run three to four feet long, though some pass seven.
britannica-1911-swordfish:
Swordfish is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a family of fishes. The family name in the text is Xiphiidae. Its chief mark is the long upper jaw of the fish. That jaw runs out into a pointed, sword-like weapon. The sword is formed from the joined bones of the upper jaw. Those bones have an extremely hard texture. The blade is shaped like a long, flattened cone.

The top of the sword is smooth to the touch. Its lower side is rough with tiny, useless teeth. The body is well shaped for fast swimming. It is long and trim, like the mackerel and tunny. The tail ends in a strong, two lobed fin. A long fin runs near the whole length of the back. The entry gives readers the build of a swift sea hunter. Form and weapon are set out part by part.
britannica-1911-whitefish:
Whitefish is a shared name applied in different countries to very different kinds of freshwater fishes, as this 1911 Britannica article explains. Many European species of one genus are often lumped under the name. The article uses it instead for the various species of the salmon-like genus Coregonus.

Those fish are somewhat herring shaped, silvery, with small toothless or weakly toothed mouths and rather large scales. They are spread over Europe, Asia, and North America, a few living in the sea but most in clear lakes. The prized lavaret of Savoy and the felchen, kilch, and gangfisch of Switzerland and southern Germany belong to this genus. So do the sik of Sweden and the houting, at times found in the North Sea off British and Irish waters.
calef-more-wonders-invisible-world-1700-:
Robert Calef, a Boston merchant, answered Cotton Mather's Wonders of the Invisible World with More Wonders of the Invisible World in 1700. Calef had watched the Salem trials and hated them. His book, in five parts, is the great contemporary demolition of the trials and of Mather's defense of them. It was printed in London, for Boston printers feared to touch it.

Calef prints the papers of the Margaret Rule case and his quarrel with the Parris household, letter against letter. He argues that spectral evidence damned the innocent and that the Mathers fed the fire. Cotton Mather called him a coal from hell, which sold the book. It is the founding skeptical record of Salem.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-act-of-settle:
The Irish Act of Settlement was passed by the Irish Parliament in 1662, after the restoration of Charles II, to settle the kingdom and pay adventurers, soldiers, and others. To grasp it and its Act of Explanation of 1664, readers must recall the Cromwellian settlement. English adventurers had advanced money for the war, and soldiers were owed large arrears of pay. To meet those claims, extirpate popery, and plant a Protestant interest, almost all Munster, Leinster, and Ulster land was confiscated.

The sorting left scarcely any Catholic, or even old Protestant, untouched. Rebels before 10 November 1642 and about a hundred named persons, including Ormond and Bishop Bramhall, were condemned to death with forfeit estates. Others who bore arms against Parliament lost their land but were promised a third of its value elsewhere. After the acts, Protestants held over two-thirds of the good land, mostly under these acts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antigonish:
Antigonish, Micmac for where the branches are torn off, is the shiretown of its Nova Scotia county. In 1886 it became a diocese of the Halifax ecclesiastical province. The first see was Arichat. The diocese takes in Nova Scotia's three easternmost counties, with all Cape Breton island. Until 1817 Nova Scotia belonged to the Quebec diocese; then it became a vicariate under Edmund Burke. William Fraser succeeded him in 1827. In 1844 the vicariate divided into Halifax and Arichat dioceses. Fraser took Arichat.

Fraser, a Valladolid Scottish College alumnus, was a strong pioneer missionary bishop. He died in 1851, succeeded in 1852 by Colin Francis MacKinnon, zealous and amiable. Failing health led MacKinnon to resign in 1877; coadjutor John Cameron became administrator. Within the diocese lies historic Louisbourg. French priests reached Acadie as early as 1604, and until Louisbourg's fall in 1758 evangelized the Micmacs, whose enduring faith attests the early Fathers' thorough work.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cush:
A scriptural entry explains Cush, a name from the ethnological table of Genesis chapter 10. It denotes a race, but is also read as an individual, the forefather of the Cushites. The land Greeks called Ethiopia is Cush in the Bible. In its widest sense it meant lands south of Assuan along the Upper Nile, now Nubia, Senaar, Kordofan, and northern Abyssinia.

More often Cush meant the kingdom of Meroe at the Nile's meeting with the Astaboras, source of the eunuch of Candace in Acts. In the eighth century BC its kings ruled Egypt, and Shabitku opposed the Assyrian Sennacherib. There were also Asian Cushites: Regma, Saba, and Dadan in Arabia, and Moses' Midianite wife is called a Cushite in the Hebrew text.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edward-walsh:
Edward Walsh was an Irish poet born near Kiskeam in County Cork in 1805 and dead at Cork in 1850. A boy of striking gifts, he taught at Millstreet and then at Tourin in County Waterford under the education commissioners. His songs appeared from 1832 to 1839, and he wrote for the Nation. Ill at ease with officials who visited his school, he moved to Dublin in 1843.

There Gavan Duffy befriended him and made him sub-editor of the Monitor. His Irish Jacobite Poetry of 1844 and Irish Popular Songs of 1847 showed a true poet, yet poverty dogged him. In 1848 he taught junior convicts on Spike Island, where John Mitchell met him on the way to penal servitude. He died within a year of taking the Cork workhouse school, and friends raised a monument to him in Irish and English.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-mush:
John Mush, alias Ratcliffe, was an English priest who chronicled the sufferings of northern Catholics and led the appellant clergy. Born in Yorkshire in 1551 or 1552, he studied six months at Douai and seven years at Rome. He was ordained and returned to England in 1583 to labor at York as confessor to Margaret Clitherow, who died for harboring him, and Francis Ingleby. Arrested and condemned in 1586, he escaped with two other priests.

A recognized leader in the north, he went to Wisbech in 1595 to arbitrate the imprisoned priests' dissensions. Then with Colleton he devised a voluntary organization to supply the want of bishops after Cardinal Allen's death. As an appellant against the archpriest he wrote the Declaratio Motuum and joined the 1602 deputation to Rome, which was refused bishops but acquitted of rebellion and schism. He later signed the 1603 protestation of allegiance and wrote Clitherow's life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-pibush:
John Pibush was an English martyr who endured years of imprisonment before his sentence was carried out. Born at Thirsk in Yorkshire, he reached Reims in 1580, took orders through 1586, and was ordained in March 1587. Sent on the English mission in January 1589, he was arrested at Morton-in-Marsh in 1593 and committed to the Gatehouse at Westminster for a year.

Tried at Gloucester under the statute against priests, he was not sentenced but returned to gaol, escaped in February 1595, was recaptured next day at Matson, and sent to the Marshalsea. Tried again at Westminster in July 1595, he was sentenced at St. Thomas's Waterings to suffer for high treason, then kept in the Queen's Bench prison for over five years. The sentence was finally executed after a single day's notice on 18 February 1601.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marash:
Marash was an Armenian Catholic diocese in a town most likely ancient Germanicia. A patriarch lived there under Alexis Comnenus, before Armenian princes took the country. Crusaders then set up a countship dependent on Edessa. Seljuks seized it in 1155, and from the sixteenth century Ottoman Turks held it.

The town stands on the slopes of Ahour-dagh, watered by streams feeding the Pyramus. It counted 52,000 people, nearly 15,000 Catholics of Armenian, Chaldean, Latin, Melchite, and Syrian rites, plus about 10,000 schismatic Christians, mostly Armenians, many tied to the American Protestant mission. Its Catholic diocese held 6,000 faithful, 12 native priests, 6 parishes or stations, and 5 schools. Armenian Sisters of the Immaculate Conception and Franciscans kept houses there. Christians suffered badly at Muslim hands in 1895 and 1909, and the town bore a very bad reputation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mush:
Mush is an Armenian Catholic see covering the sanjaks of Mush and Seert in the vilayet of Bitlis. It was created by Leo XIII in 1883, counting about 5,000 faithful, 7 secular priests, 7 churches or chapels, 5 schools and a house of the Venetian Mechitarists. Its chief stations beyond Mush include neighbouring villages such as Bitlis and Van.

The town, built by an Armenian prince named Muchigh, stands on a hill below a ruined citadel amid vineyards. Below stretches a well-tilled plain fifty miles long by eighteen wide. Some 27,000 people live there, including 3,000 Armenian Catholics, 10,000 Armenian schismatics and 700 Protestants, the rest Muslims. The country, though healthy and fairly rich, suffers constant Kurdish and nomad raids that terrorise the Christians.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-parish:
A parish is a part of a diocese under a priest duly appointed to secure the helps of religion for the faithful living there. The faithful are parishioners, the priest parochus, curate, parish priest, or pastor. Forming a parish needs a body of faithful under pastoral rule, usually fixed by territory under the priest's sole jurisdiction, since Trent ordered parish bounds to be defined. Domicile, quasi-domicile, or a month's residence makes a parishioner.

Territory need not be exclusive: parishes can overlap by rite or nationality, as in the East or great American cities, and rare parishes gather families without territory. Early city and country churches grew under bishops, with country priests and village chorepiscopi by 320. Later pages treat pastors, rectors of missions, removable and irremovable, their rights, duties, and support, and the mother-church bonds that tie parishes to cathedrals.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-patrick-walsh:
Patrick Walsh was an American journalist and United States senator born at Ballingary in County Limerick on 1 January 1840 and dead at Augusta, Georgia, on 19 March 1900. Emigrating with his parents to Charleston, South Carolina, in 1852, he was apprenticed to a printer, attended night school, and saved enough to enter Georgetown College in 1859. Civil War sent him home to Charleston in 1861, where he joined the militia as lieutenant of the Meagher Guards.

In 1862 he moved to Augusta and joined the Constitutionalist staff. That began a thirty-two-year press career through the Pacificator, Banner of the South, and Chronicle and Sentinel. He bought the last in 1877 and merged it with the Constitutionalist. He served as Associated Press agent, state legislator, Democratic convention delegate, and Columbian Fair commissioner. Appointed senator in April 1894, he was then elected to the same seat.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-walsh:
Peter Walsh was an Irish Franciscan who broke with Rome over loyalty to the crown, born at Mooretown about 1608. Educated and ordained at the Irish College of St. Anthony at Louvain, he backed the Ormondists at Kilkenny, became their guardian in 1648, fought the nuncio Rinuccini's censures, and served as chaplain to the Munster army until its defeat. After wandering years, the Restoration brought him to London in Ormonde's favour.

As agent for the surviving Irish bishops from 1661, he pressed the Remonstrance, a declaration of civil loyalty that split Ireland for years. At a Dublin meeting of bishops and clergy in June 1666 he failed to win signatures for a text most judged disrespectful to the Holy See. Breaking with church authority, he led a small party called the Valesians, a worry to bishops for years. He died in London in 1688.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-robert-walsh:
Robert Walsh was an American publicist and diplomat who helped give the young republic a serious press. Born at Baltimore in 1785, he was among the first students at Georgetown College, graduating in 1801 and starting law. During two years in Europe he wrote on American institutions for Paris and London papers. Back home in 1808, he was admitted to the bar, and in 1811 founded the American Review of History and Politics at Philadelphia, the first American quarterly.

His Appeal from the Judgment of Great Britain respecting the United States of 1819 won thanks from the Pennsylvania legislature. From 1821 to 1836 he edited the Philadelphia National Gazette, devoted to politics, science, and letters, lifting American journalism by knowledge and taste. Lord Jeffrey praised his letters on the French government. He published Didactics in 1836 and served as Consul General at Paris from 1837 to 1844, remaining there until his death in 1859. His house drew learned men.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-symbolism-of-:
Among early Christian symbols, the fish ranks first in importance, and this entry explains why. Pagan art had long used the fish as mere decoration. Clement of Alexandria, born about 150, already urged readers to engrave seals with a dove or a fish, without bothering to explain either sign. Catacomb paintings show the symbol in use decades earlier.

Its fame rests chiefly on a Greek acrostic: the initials of Jesus Christ, Son of God, Saviour spell Ichthys, the word for fish. Born perhaps at Alexandria as a protest against emperors styled Son of God, it became a brief creed. After the fourth century the symbol faded, surviving only as ornament on fonts and cups.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-walsh:
Thomas Walsh, a Catholic bishop born in London in October 1777, built up the Church in the Midlands in a time of growth. His father, an Irish merchant, died in his infancy, and his Protestant mother sent him to St. Albans grammar school. An uncle, a priest, got him into St. Omer's college, where his faith was saved, and he shared the imprisonment at Dourlens before finishing at Old Hall Green.

Walsh served Bishop Milner as chaplain, became vice-president of Oscott in 1808 and president from 1818 to 1826, and was consecrated titular Bishop of Cambysopolis in 1825 as Milner's coadjutor. Succeeding Milner in 1826, he oversaw the building of St. Mary's College, Oscott, and the cathedrals of Birmingham and Nottingham. Translated to London in 1848 against his wishes, he left administration to his coadjutor and died in February 1849.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-walsh:
William Walsh was Bishop of Meath who lost his see and freedom rather than swear Elizabeth's supremacy. Born at Dunboyne about 1512, he died at Alcalá de Henares on 4 January 1577. He joined the Cistercians at Bective, studied at Oxford to a divinity doctorate, and fled the suppressions of 1536 and 1537 abroad. He became chaplain to Cardinal Pole at Rome and prior of the suppressed houses of Dulchek and Colpe.

Returning with Pole as legate, Walsh joined the 1554 commission stripping married clergy and took Meath itself on 18 October 1554. Under Elizabeth he fought the new liturgy in Convocation, preached against the Prayer Book at Trim, and on 4 February 1560 refused the supremacy oath, losing his temporalities and his liberty. Freed after eighteen months, he won papal reappointment in 1564, was jailed again in Dublin Castle in 1565, escaped to Nantes in 1572, and died at Alcalá among Cistercian brethren.
children-of-the-bush:
Henry Lawson's Children of the Bush gathers stories and sketches of Australian bush life. It opens with the creed of the bush itself: pass the hat for a man in trouble, jailbird or gentleman alike.

Contents include Send Round the Hat, That Pretty Girl in the Army, and Lord Douglas. Two Sundowners, A Sketch of Mateship, A Bush Publican's Lament, The Shearer's Dream, and The Bush-Fire follow. Lawson writes of shearers, sundowners, drovers and publicans with humour, mateship and a sharp eye for hardship. Readers who want the real Australia of the 1890s, in its own voice, will find Lawson unsurpassed.
doe-osti-2583498-hyblend-collaborative-r:
The HyBlend partnership, closed out in report NREL/TP-7A10-94949 dated March 27, 2025, was a four-laboratory attack on one question: can hydrogen ride in America's natural gas pipelines? Todd Deutsch was NREL's contact. Blending hydrogen into the existing network could move clean fuel without new pipes, if the pipes survive it. Sandia, Pacific Northwest, Argonne, and NREL each took a quarter of the problem.

Sandia studied metals, asking how hydrogen and gas impurities degrade steel pipeline integrity. Pacific Northwest took polymers, the plastic pipes and seals of distribution networks, and their lifetime under blends. Argonne ran life cycle analysis across hydrogen pathways. NREL priced it all, techno-economic analysis of producing hydrogen and blending it versus the alternatives. The four objectives share one theme: impurities and materials decide feasibility long before policy does. HyBlend's structure matched a problem that refuses to sit inside a single discipline.
doe-osti-2588289-high-fidelity-simulatio:
Cory Stack and Ross Wagnild of Sandia National Laboratories wrote this report, SAND2025-11076, printed September 2025, on high-fidelity simulation of a Mach 9 shock and turbulent boundary layer interaction. When a shock wave strikes a turbulent boundary layer at hypersonic speed, the flow can separate, unsteady loads spike, and heating concentrates. Designers of hypersonic vehicles need those loads predicted, not guessed.

The team ran large eddy simulations and compared them with wall-modeled versions, which trade resolution near the wall for speed.
