Instantaneous flowfields, mean wall shear stress, heat flux, and pressure are mapped across the interaction region. The wall-modeled cases grow a larger separation region, which pushes shock impingement further downstream on the ramp. Unsteady behavior gets its own treatment: root-mean-square wall pressure fluctuations and their power spectra, compared between the full and wall-modeled runs at chosen locations.
doe-osti-3002176-optimizing-control-for-:
Yiyuan Qiao, Zhenning Li, Mitchell Ishmael, and Xiaobing Liu close out CRADA project NFE-24-10403 in Oak Ridge report ORNL/TM-2025/4135, dated August 2025. The project tuned controls for building cooling systems fitted with thermal energy storage. Stored chilled water or ice lets a building shift its cooling load away from peak price hours. The work targeted existing heating and cooling plants, not new designs.

Two control styles were compared. Rule-based control follows fixed simple rules and proved cheap to run and easy to deploy soon. Model predictive control plans ahead with forecasts and cut costs further in tests. The authors recommend field trials of the storage system next. They also suggest widening the predictive control to balance cost, comfort, and peak load together.
doe-osti-3012212-design-and-validation-o:
A nanosecond short wave infrared streak camera built around a galvanometer mirror is built and tested in a Los Alamos report by Nicolas Berube, Kyle Thurmond, and John Bowlan. The compact system replaces tube based streak cameras with a mirror driven by a galvanometer and a multiple reflection optical path. Time resolution reached 139.5 nanoseconds per pixel.

Tests used hydrogen oxygen argon detonations in a modular tube at the University of Central Florida. Image slope gives wave velocity. Mixtures from 10 to 60 percent argon showed intensity rise and decay trends as expected. Filtered setups were limited by lens losses and detector sensitivity, but the design showed promise for reactive environments.
doe-osti-3028141-carbon-utilization-and-:
Robert Balch of the New Mexico Institute of Mining and Technology led the Carbon Utilization and Storage Partnership of the Western United States under award DE-FE0031837, from October 2019 to September 2025. George El-kaseeh, Jennifer Raney, and Brian McPherson joined him. The partnership mapped where the West could store carbon dioxide and use it, state by state and basin by basin. This final report is very large, a regional evidence base rather than a single study.

Modeling chapters simulate injection histories in detail. One Arbuckle aquifer case first mimics years of legacy brine disposal, then runs thirty years with wastewater and carbon dioxide injected together, then closes with wastewater-only periods of ten or sixty years. Simulator output was written as binary files, reference variables at every time step and plot variables at chosen times, then converted for analysis.
feijoo-cartas-eruditas-tomo-1-1773-spani:
After the Teatro Crítico, Benito Jerónimo Feijóo y Montenegro carried his work into letters. Tomo Primero of the Cartas Eruditas, y Curiosas gathers the first of them, in the 1773 edition, in Spanish. The title promises learned and curious letters, and the form let Feijóo answer real questions from real readers.

In letter after letter he knocks down common errors and superstitions with calm, sourced argument. The topics shift as his mail shifted, but the test stays the same: what proof stands behind the claim? The Cartas complete his great skeptical project in a warmer, more direct voice. They show a teacher answering his country one letter at a time.
feijoo-cartas-eruditas-tomo-2-1773-spani:
Tomo Segundo, the second volume of the Cartas Eruditas, y Curiosas, appears in the 1773 edition, in Spanish. Its author, Benito Jerónimo Feijóo y Montenegro, had turned from long discourses to letters. Correspondents sent him the doubts and tales of the day, and he replied in print for all to read.

The letters in this volume go on clearing away errors and superstitions of many kinds. Feijóo treats each report with care, then shows where the proof fails or the tale grew in the telling. The set as a whole completes his skeptical life's work. This volume keeps the same patient method in a brisker, more personal form.
feijoo-cartas-eruditas-tomo-3-1773-spani:
Benito Jerónimo Feijóo y Montenegro's Cartas Eruditas, y Curiosas reaches Tomo Tercero in the 1773 edition, written in Spanish. Feijóo was a Benedictine monk whose essays and letters made him Spain's best known foe of untested belief. The Cartas carried forward the design of his earlier Teatro Crítico Universal.

These letters answer questions, reports, and rumors with sourced, steady reasoning. Claims of wonders and strange cures meet requests for proof, and many quietly fall apart. Feijóo's tone stays kind toward the asker and firm toward the error. Together the five volumes of letters round out the most trusted critical voice of the Spanish Enlightenment.
feijoo-cartas-eruditas-tomo-4-1773-spani:
Tomo Quarto is the fourth volume of the Cartas Eruditas, y Curiosas by Benito Jerónimo Feijóo y Montenegro, here in the 1773 edition. The letters, in Spanish, continue the plan of his Teatro Crítico: test the beliefs that people repeat without checking. Feijóo wrote as a monk, a scholar, and a public teacher at once.

The letters in this volume take up new errors and superstitions sent in by readers. Each reply weighs the claim, names the weak point in its proof, and offers a calmer account. The effect builds across the set: doubt used with care becomes a form of honesty. This volume shows that method still sharp in Feijóo's later years.
feijoo-cartas-eruditas-tomo-5-1773-spani:
With Tomo Quinto, the fifth volume of the Cartas Eruditas, y Curiosas, Benito Jerónimo Feijóo y Montenegro completes his letters. The 1773 edition presents them in Spanish. Across two great sets of writings, the Teatro and the Cartas, Feijóo had spent decades answering the errors of his age.

The final letters still do the same steady work: a claim arrives, and Feijóo asks for its proof. Superstitions and common errors that fail the test are set aside without anger or fuss. A reader who ends here has seen the whole arc of his project. It remains the fullest statement of calm doubt in Spanish letters.
feijoo-teatro-critico-tomo-1-1773-spanis:
Benito Jerónimo Feijóo y Montenegro was a Spanish monk and scholar who set out to free his country from common errors. Tomo Primero, the first volume of his Teatro Crítico Universal, appears here in the Madrid edition of 1773. The work is written in Spanish as a set of essays, called discourses.

Each discourse takes up some belief held without proof, from false miracles to tales of wonders and prodigies. Feijóo tests such claims with calm reason and wide reading. His goal, summed up in the Spanish word desengaño, was to undo false ideas. The volume opened the great skeptical work of the Spanish Enlightenment.
feijoo-teatro-critico-tomo-2-1773-spanis:
Tomo Segundo is the second volume of the Teatro Crítico Universal by Benito Jerónimo Feijóo y Montenegro. It appears here in the Madrid edition of 1773, in Spanish. Feijóo, a monk and scholar, had won a wide public by questioning beliefs that most people never stopped to test.

The discourses in this volume keep up his campaign against common errors and superstition. He examines claims of miracles, wonders, and prodigies, and asks what proof stands behind each one. The plain, steady tone is the point: reason, used with patience, can clear away fear. This volume deepens the work that made Feijóo central to Spain's Enlightenment.
feijoo-teatro-critico-tomo-3-1773-spanis:
In Tomo Tercero, the third volume of his Teatro Crítico Universal, Benito Jerónimo Feijóo y Montenegro presses on with his life's task. The Madrid edition of 1773 presents the essays in Spanish. Feijóo wrote for readers across Spain who trusted old tales more than they trusted their own judgment.

His discourses here take up fresh cases of error, superstition, and false wonder. In each one he weighs the tale, checks the proof, and shows where belief ran ahead of fact. The set as a whole became the base skeptical work in the Spanish tongue. This third volume shows the method fully formed and at work.
feijoo-teatro-critico-tomo-4-1773-spanis:
Tomo Quarto, printed at Madrid in 1773, is the fourth volume of Benito Jerónimo Feijóo y Montenegro's Teatro Crítico Universal. Feijóo was the best known Spanish critic of false belief in the 1700s. His essays, written in Spanish, were read far beyond the schools and cloisters of his day.

The discourses gathered here go on exposing common errors in field after field. Superstition, false miracles, and popular tales of prodigies all face the same calm test of proof. Feijóo never mocks the reader; he teaches the reader to ask for reasons. That patient habit is why the Teatro stayed a force in Spanish thought.
feijoo-teatro-critico-tomo-5-1773-spanis:
Benito Jerónimo Feijóo y Montenegro's Teatro Crítico Universal reaches its fifth volume in Tomo Quinto, here in the Madrid edition of 1773. The Spanish essays carry on the plan set out in the first volume. Feijóo, a Benedictine monk, spent years answering the false notions of his age in print.

Volume five brings more discourses against errors that passed from mouth to mouth as truth. False miracles, prodigies, and groundless fears are set against sober proof and common sense. Read in order, the volumes train a habit of doubt that checks before it believes. Read alone, this one still shows Feijóo's clear voice at full strength.
feijoo-teatro-critico-tomo-6-1765-spanis:
Tomo Sexto, the sixth volume of the Teatro Crítico Universal, comes from the Madrid edition of 1765. Its author, Benito Jerónimo Feijóo y Montenegro, was a Spanish monk whose essays taught a nation to test what it heard. The Spanish word for his aim was desengaño, a freeing from false ideas.

The discourses in this volume range across the errors and wonders of common talk. Feijóo weighs reports of miracles and prodigies and finds the proof wanting, again and again. He writes with respect for faith but none for fraud or fear. By volume six his method was famous, and readers trusted the test he applied.
feijoo-teatro-critico-tomo-7-1773-spanis:
Printed at Madrid in 1773, Tomo Septimo is the seventh volume of Benito Jerónimo Feijóo y Montenegro's Teatro Crítico Universal. Feijóo's essays in Spanish formed the best known work of doubt and testing in his country's Enlightenment. Each volume stands as a set of discourses that a reader can open at almost any point.

In this volume the discourses keep after the same foes: common errors, superstition, and wonders believed without proof. Feijóo asks who saw the thing, who told the tale, and what other cause might explain it. Those plain questions did quiet, lasting work. They helped shift Spanish letters toward fact, measure, and calm judgment.
feijoo-teatro-critico-tomo-8-1773-spanis:
Tomo Octavo, from the Madrid edition of 1773, is the eighth volume of Benito Jerónimo Feijóo y Montenegro's Teatro Crítico Universal. Feijóo, a Spanish Benedictine monk, had built his fame on essays that test common belief. The Teatro was the chief skeptical work of the Spanish Enlightenment, written in Spanish for a broad public.

The discourses in this late volume still pursue errors, superstitions, and false miracles wherever they hide. Feijóo brings proof, source, and plain sense to bear on each claim in turn. A reader finishing the set has watched one mind work through the fears of an age. The habit of testing, more than any single verdict, is the gift.
foes-in-ambush:
King rides with the cavalry in Foes in Ambush, dated 1893. Charles King, a captain in the United States Army, sets his tale in Arizona. The sun goes down like a hissing globe of fire over the desert. A paymaster's ambulance, its safe dumped at dawn, throws a mile-long shadow across the flat before the corral.

The sampled pages give the young officer Drummond his orders and his measure. Barely twenty-three, he had entered West Point at seventeen and wore a fine record. He sends men to join the sergeant, with a warning not to be seen from the front. Then he draws his Colt and checks its loaded chambers with care. A sister with many needs and few means clouds his young life. King's tale is army fiction from inside the ranks.
garrison-s-finish:
W. B. M. Ferguson subtitled this novel a romance of the race-course, and it opens on a jockey at the bottom of his fall. Garrison, once the popular idol of the turf, has lost the Carter Handicap and expects the Jockey Club to revoke his licence. The crowd believes what the sporting papers hint: that he has gone crooked, throwing races in league with his owner.

Ferguson follows the disgraced rider through the world that made and dropped him. Bookmakers, owners, and the few friends who stuck by him crowd the chapters. The question the book sets is whether a man marked as a cheat can ride one straight race that matters and win back his name. It is a sporting melodrama of disgrace and one last finish, written close to the paddock.
gourlay-an-appeal-to-the-common-sense-mi:
Robert Gourlay, a Scot who had stirred reform in Upper Canada, published this appeal at London in 1826. The title page states his case in brief: he writes, he says, now and for the last two years imprisoned without fair examination or trial. He dedicates the sheets to his children, as the place to declare his principles. A verse on long years of outrage and imputed madness heads the appeal.

Gourlay lays out his treatment by officials in Canada and Britain, and calls on the common sense and manhood of the nation to judge it. The book is long, heated, and full of documents and grievances. Gourlay was a flawed man, yet his charges touched real abuses in colonial rule. The appeal stands as a raw record of how an agitator fought the state with print when other doors were shut.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-AMLASH_AMLASH: AMLASH was a CIA cryptonym for a Cuban asset drawn into the agency's plots to kill Fidel Castro, among the most sensitive operations of the Kennedy years. This file holds government material filed under that cryptonym alone, released without a fuller description. Even its bare title ties it to the assassination plots that the Church Committee later exposed to public view. The record is kept as issued, a fragment of the paper trail left by the Castro plots.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-PosnerScholarsS:
A second critique of Gerald Posner's 'Case Closed' takes a different method from its companion piece. This writer quotes the book directly and disputes its treatment of witnesses and evidence. The examples named include Delgado and Kerry Thornley, two men from Oswald's Marine and New Orleans years.

Where the other critique attacks the book's publicity, this one works the footnotes. Witness by witness, it asks whether Posner quoted fairly and weighed honestly. Thornley matters because he knew Oswald and later became a figure in the Garrison inquiry. Delgado matters as a Marine witness to Oswald's shooting and talk. The critique is scholarship as combat, and it preserves the researchers' counter-case in their own detailed form.
guazzo-compendium-maleficarum-1929-engli:
Francesco Maria Guazzo, an Italian friar, wrote his Compendium Maleficarum at Milan in 1608. It became one of the standard handbooks for hunting witches. English readers got it only in 1929, in E. A. Ashwin's translation, with notes by editor Montague Summers.

Across three books, Guazzo sorts demons into classes and lists their powers. He covers pacts with the devil, poisons, curses, and the signs judges should look for. He also gives cures and prayers meant to break spells. Historians read it to see how witch belief worked in practice. Ashwin's version made the full text open to English readers for the first time.
hard-cash:
Charles Reade published Hard Cash in 1863, a novel with a cause. In a letter of 1868 printed at the front he answers the charge of mere sensation. Without sensation, he says, there can be no interest. But his plan is to mix character and philosophy with the sensational element. The prologue opens in a snowy villa outside the seaport of Barkington, where Mrs. Dodd lives with her son Edward, aged twenty, and her daughter Julia.

Edward Dodd's tale turns on a sum of hard cash, a bank failure, and a plot that lands him, sane, in a private lunatic asylum. Reade had campaigned against the abuses of such asylums, and the novel is his evidence dressed as story. The pace is fierce and the villains are hissable. It remains a prime sample of the Victorian sensation novel with a reformer's fist inside it.
hereward-the-last-of-the-english:
Charles Kingsley wrote this historical novel about Hereward, an English outlaw. Hereward is cast out young and seeks his fortune abroad. He fights bears, serves kings, and wins famed armor. Then word comes that the Normans have crushed England at Hastings.

The long chapter list turns home: Hereward gathers an army in the fens. He clears Bourne of Frenchmen and holds out as a last English chief. Kingsley fills the tale with battles, voyages, and rough fen folk. Readers get a stirring, patriotic take on the years right after the Conquest.
historic-tales-the-romance-of-reality-vo:
Charles Morris devoted this fourth volume of Historic Tales to England. The tales start with how England became Christian. Alfred and the Danes, the wooing of Elfrida, and the end of Saxon England follow. A plate of Warwick Castle fronts the book.

Hereward the Wake and Robin Hood stand among the heroes. Wallace and Bruce carry the Scots' fight for freedom. Later tales reach the Black Prince, Wat Tyler, and the Wars of the Roses. One scene shows a young pretender crushed by Henry the Seventh. Morris serves English history as vivid story, picked for peril and color.

Charles Morris gave this seventh volume of Historic Tales to Spain itself. A plate shows the Emperor Charles the Fifth in retreat at Yuste. The tales begin in the old Gothic kingdom, with good King Wamba. Enchanted palaces and the battle of the Guadalete follow.

Bernardo del Carpio and Ruy Diaz, the Cid, stand among the heroes. Las Navas de Tolosa and the fall of Granada mark the Moorish wars' end. Columbus returns in triumph near the close. Peter the Cruel and the Great Captain add blood and skill. Morris tells Spain's past as high romance, full of kings, keys, and last sighs.
how-to-cook-fish:
Olive Green, the pen name of Myrtle Reed, wrote this fish cookbook. The contents alone show its scale. Eleven court bouillons and one hundred simple fish sauces open the book. Then the fish come one by one, each with its count of ways.

Bass gets forty-five ways, codfish sixty-seven, and halibut eighty. Frog legs, finnan haddie, and pompano all have their chapters. Salmon à la suprême and salmon pudding show the style: brief, plain, exact. Season and freshness are treated before a single recipe. Cooks of the day got a whole fish kitchen between two covers.
inaugural-address-of-franklin-delano-roo:
Franklin Delano Roosevelt gave this inaugural address in Washington on March 4, 1933, at the depth of the Great Depression, and the hosted text is the speech in full. Banks were failing across the country, and a banking holiday shadowed the day. Roosevelt opens with the line that made the speech famous: the only thing Americans have to fear is fear itself.

He blames the money changers for the collapse, promises work through public action, and warns that he will ask Congress for war-like powers if the crisis demands them. He also pledges a good neighbor policy toward the world. The speech's calm nerve helped steady the country, and the New Deal push of his first hundred days followed at once.
isopel-berners-the-history-of-certain-do:
George Borrow told of Isopel Berners in a Staffordshire dingle in July 1825, in this 1901 edition. Thomas Seccombe edited the episode from Borrow's autobiography, with introduction and notes. Borrow was born at East Dereham in Norfolk, the introduction recalls. Cowper, England's pious bard, rests in the same town, it notes.

Belle, as Isopel is called, rebukes a postillion who guesses she ran away for love. Mind how you get on, friend, she says in a deep serious tone. Gypsy life, boxing, and talk fill the dingle camp. The episode is a famed slice of Lavengro's world.
laicus-or-the-experiences-of-a-layman-in:
Lyman Abbott published Laicus in New York in 1872. Its subtitle gives the experiences of a layman in a country parish. The fictional parish is called Wheathedge.

The narrator explains how he came to Wheathedge and joined its church. Chapters treat church finances, Bible scholars, and a pastor's resignation. A supply committee hunts for a new minister, with some comedy. Christmas at Wheathedge brings a warmer chapter. Abbott uses story form to explore real questions about congregational life and lay duty. Abbott later became a well-known editor and minister. His fiction here argues for thoughtful, active lay church members.
lectures-on-language-as-particularly-con:
William Stevens Balch wrote these lectures on language and English grammar. Transcribers kept his small capitals and bracketed words from the original. The book treats speech as a subject fit for public lectures.

Balch connects general language study with English in particular. Grammar, in his hands, explains how words do their work. Nineteenth-century lecturers carried such teaching to towns across America. Students of English history can see older grammar ideas here. His plain lecture style suits readers meeting the subject fresh. Balch's brackets show an author revising as he printed. Such marks let readers watch a lecturer think on paper.
life-in-the-clearings-versus-the-bush:
Susanna Moodie contrasts settled clearings with the rough bush here. She dedicates the book to her husband, sheriff of Hastings County. Contents begin with Belleville and local improvements. Sketches of society, free schools, and amusements follow in turn.

Chapters treat camp meetings, mourning customs, and odd characters. Toronto, a lunatic asylum, and an agricultural show widen the view. Grace Marks appears among the character studies. Moodie writes as an attached friend and wife, from inside Upper Canada. A travelling musician's trials and a singing master lighten the sketches. Lost children and odd characters give Belleville its human variety.
maier-themis-aurea-1656-english:
Michael Maier wrote Themis Aurea, the laws of the Fraternity of the Rosie Crosse, in Latin in 1618. N. L. translated it, and this London edition of 1656 is the first English version. Maier sets out how the brethren govern themselves: their rules of life, healing, and secrecy, framed as the laws of a hidden order.

The laws require the brethren to heal the sick freely and to keep their fellowship secret. Maier presents the fraternity as a medical and moral college. His document carried Rosicrucian organization theory into England. Whatever the brethren's reality, the Themis gave later orders a constitution to imitate. English readers of 1656 met the Rose Cross here as a rule-bound society, not a rumor.
mather-cases-of-conscience-1693-english:
Increase Mather, the leading minister of Massachusetts, published Cases of Conscience Concerning Evil Spirits Personating Men in 1693. The Salem trials were still hot, and Mather's book threw cold water on them. Its famous line holds that it were better ten suspected witches escape than one innocent person be condemned. The ministers of the colony issued it as their joint guidance.

Mather argues that the devil can wear the shape of an innocent, so spectral sight alone cannot hang a soul. The book helped end the trials, for the court itself had asked the ministers' counsel. Mather was Cotton Mather's father, and the son took a harder line. The father's caution reads now as the voice of reason in a panic.
nasa-tm-19700028255-use-of-low-constant-:
Quintin Peasley and Lester Katz of the Space Sciences Laboratory wrote this report on September 16, 1969. It comes from the Marshall Space Flight Center in Alabama. It studies how a low, steady thrust can carry a spacecraft from one orbit to another without any single large burn.

The authors build a fuel-minimized path that meets set starting and finishing conditions. Their test case moves a constantly thrusting craft from an elliptical orbit around Mars into a lower circular one. The method suits electric ion-propelled spacecraft, which push gently for very long stretches. Such craft could start in either an elliptical or circular orbit and power themselves to a chosen circular height.
oddsfish:
Robert Hugh Benson published the historical novel Oddsfish! in 1914. The story starts on May 1, 1678, in Rome. The narrator is taken to meet Pope Innocent the Eleventh. His adventures then move to the courts of England and France. Benson says he checked plots and places with care.

The novel treats the last years of King Charles the Second. It includes political plots and movements of that time. Benson claims the king says and does only attested things. Fiction enters where the narrator meets invented people. The book blends romance, faith, and court intrigue. The prologue begins in heat, cloisters, and Vatican halls.
old-french-romances-done-into-english:
William Morris turned old French romances into English here. George Allen published the book in London in 1896. Joseph Jacobs wrote the introduction to the volume. The tales first appeared from the Kelmscott Press. Morris loved medieval stories and retold them with care.

Jacobs says Morris alone could match the medieval tone. The versions keep the color and charm of the originals. Readers meet knights, lovers, and wonders from old France. The tales had grown rare and hard to find. This cheaper edition saved them for wider reading. It remains a fine doorway into medieval romance.
poets-and-dreamers-studies-and-translati:
Lady Gregory published Poets and Dreamers in Dublin and New York in 1903, subtitled studies and translations from the Irish. Gregory, co-founder of the Abbey Theatre, spent years collecting songs and stories from Irish-speaking people around her Galway home, and this book is the harvest. Essays on the blind poet Raftery, on west Irish ballads and Jacobite ballads, and translations of poems by Douglas Hyde, called An Craoibhin, the little branch.

Later chapters turn stranger and sadder: mountain theology, herb healing, the wandering tribe, and workhouse dreams, the visions of the very poor. A dedication to Trinity College undergraduates, headed by Whitman's lines about finding the best in folks nearest to you, states her faith plainly. The book helped invent the Irish literary revival's idea of the peasant west, and its translations still carry the music of a vanishing oral world.
practical-exercises-in-english:
Huber Gray Buehler, master in English at the Hotchkiss School. Arranged his Practical Exercises in English for use with Adams Sherman Hill's Foundations of Rhetoric, the Harvard textbook that defined college composition teaching. The American Book Company issued the workbook, copyrighted in 1895 by Harper and Brothers. Where Hill laid down principles, Buehler supplied the drills: chapter after chapter of sentences to diagnose, correct, and punctuate.

Contents march through the parts of speech as Hill ordered them: good use, articles, nouns. Pronouns, verbs at greatest length, adjectives and adverbs, prepositions, and conjunctions, with an appendix and index. The first chapter asks why one word is not as good as another, and answers with passages from the King James Bible. Generations of schoolboys learned correctness from such pairings of rule and exercise; Buehler's book is the gymnasium built beside Hill's lecture hall.
punky-dunk-and-the-gold-fish:
Punky Dunk and the Gold Fish is a short picture book in verse for young children, published in Chicago by P. F. Volland and Company with a 1912 copyright. No author is named; the story and pictures are offered to a good little child whose name is left blank on the title page.

Punky Dunk is a fat black and white kitten with black on his nose, toes, tail, and ears. He sleeps in a box of straw and drinks his milk. He watches two things with care. One is the bird in its brass cage. The other is the gold fish at play in their clear glass bowl.
representation-of-the-impiety-and-immora:
The Augustan Reprint Society issued this number in March 1947, as number two of its third series, Essays on the Stage. It reprints two anonymous pieces of 1704 on the English stage and its morals. Emmett L. Avery supplies an introduction, with a bibliographical note.

The first piece is the Representation of the Impiety and Immorality of the English Stage itself, a charge in its very title. The second is Some Thoughts Concerning the Stage, from the same year. Society pages around the reprint price membership at two dollars and fifty cents for six issues a year. The number sold alone for seventy-five cents.
robbery-under-arms-a-story-of-life-and-a:
Thomas Alexander Browne, who wrote as Rolf Boldrewood, tells this story of life and adventure in the Australian bush and goldfields. A preface to the new edition, dated at Melbourne on December 12, 1888, dedicates the tale to R. Murray Smith. Boldrewood calls it an ower true tale of the wilder aspects of Australian life.

Though dressed as fiction, the chronicle of the Marston family is not wholly fanciful, he insists. Much of it is literally true and can be checked in official records. Chapter one brings Dick Marston forward: a Sydney-side native of twenty-nine, six feet tall, who can ride anything lapped in horsehide, swim like a musk-duck, and track with the best.
roughing-it-in-the-bush: Susanna Moodie wrote Roughing It in the Bush, and she gave the book to her sister Agnes Strickland, author of Lives of the Queens of England. She gave it as a mark of love. The contents list twenty chapters, opening with A Visit to Grosse Isle, Quebec, and Our Journey up the Country. Later titles include Our First Settlement, Uncle Joe and His Family, The Village Hotel, The Land-Jobber, and A Journey to the Woods. Later titles include The Wilderness and Our Indian Friendsand Our Logging-Bee.
stories-by-foreign-authors-spanish:
Spanish, in the Stories by Foreign Authors set, is dated 1898. It holds two tales by Alarcon, The Tall Woman and Moors and Christians. Selgas's White Butterfly and Becquer's Organist follow. Caballero's Bread Cast Upon the Waters closes the set. Rollo Ogden made the English version of The Tall Woman.

Alarcon's tale is told by Gabriel, an engineer, resting under a pine near a spring on the crest of the Guadarrama, about a league and a half from the Escurial. He promises a strange tale to prove how little men really know. Ghosts, old wars, and church music fill the rest.
the-christmas-books-of-mr-m-a-titmarsh:
William Makepeace Thackeray published these Christmas books under his pen name, Mr. M. A. Titmarsh. The contents gather Mrs. Perkins's Ball, Our Street, Dr. Birch and his Young Friends, and The Kickleburys on the Rhine. A fairy tale closes the set: The Rose and the Ring, the history of Prince Giglio and Prince Bulbo.

Mrs. Perkins's Ball opens with the Mulligan of Ballymulligan, whose home town nobody can place. The narrator once asked and got a look of ferocious dignity, plus a sharp word about Saxon curiosity. He never pressed the point again, since it hardly matters where the Celtic principality lies. The Mulligan's town address is just as vague: he points down toward Oxbridge with his big stick and says he lives there. Letters reach him at friends' houses, and parcels wait at taverns he frequents. Thackeray's holiday humor runs on such social sketches.
the-circus-boys-on-the-mississippi-or-af: Edgar B. P. Darlington sent his circus boys down the big river in this tale, subtitled Afloat with the Big Show on the Big River. Project Gutenberg issued the text in January 2001, etext 2477, prepared by Greg Berckes. Only the Gutenberg header stands here, though, with its copyright and donation notices. The river voyage itself never begins in what is present.
the-fathers-of-the-constitution-a-chroni:
Max Farrand wrote The Fathers of the Constitution for the Chronicles of America series, printed by Yale in 1921. The full texts of the Declaration, the Articles, the Northwest Ordinance, and the Constitution stand at the back.

Farrand starts with the peace treaty that ended the war, then takes up trade, the weak Confederation, and the dark days before the convention. He tells how the Federal Convention met, did its work, and set the Union on firm ground. The book gives lay readers a clear, short road from a loose league of states to one nation under a written frame.
the-glugs-of-gosh:
C. J. Dennis wrote The Glugs of Gosh. It was first published in 1917. Pictures are by Hal Gye. The contents list thirteen parts. They run from The Glug Quest and Joi, the Glug, to The Stones of Gosh. They name Sym, the son of Joi, and The Swanks of Gosh. They name The Seer, The Debate, and The Little Red Dog.

An opening rhyme gives the way to meet a Glug: hairs from a rabbit-skin rug, blown south and west, and a third one burned and swallowed. Whoever calls that fool's talk is a Glug of the old Gosh school, and will climb a tree in an east wind just to show he knows. The nonsense verse sets the comic, rhyming tone of the whole tale.
the-honorable-senator-sage-brush: Francis Lynde wrote The Honorable Senator Sage-Brush, published in New York by Charles Scribner's Sons in 1913. A dedication to Mr. George Ady calls him the author's teacher in the school of western railroading and a keen observer of the conditions the book seeks to portray. The contents begin with Because Patricia Said No, The Boss, and A False Gallop of Memories. Only the title page, dedication, and the start of the contents are present here.
the-kiltartan-poetry-book-prose-translat:
Lady Gregory's introduction to her prose translations begins with childhood reading. Asked to name an Irish poem, the child chose a Thomas Moore melody. Guests sang such songs at the piano. The only Moore volume on the table was Lalla Rookh. She remembers vexing her governess with Malachi's collar of gold. Both believed the proud invader English. The collar had been torn from him, the song said.

A love of country woke in her through her home's beauty. Burren and Iar Connacht showed from its hillsides. Her old nurse sympathized with the rebels of 1798. Gregory spent her Bible-lesson sixpences at Loughrea on Fenian books. She became the stationer's best customer for them. A sister copied a scornful line about patriotism into her birthday book. The translations grow from that early hunger. She wanted the real tradition behind Moore's faint sentiment.
the-land-of-the-black-mountain-the-adven: Reginald Wyon and Gerald Prance traveled in Montenegro and issued their account first in 1903, with a cheaper issue in 1905. Only the front pages and the start of the contents are present here, noting fifty-one illustrations and a dedication to Prince Nicolas of Montenegro. The first chapter summary promises geography, character, honesty, patriotism, and love of arms. The journey narrative itself does not appear in this record.
the-memoirs-of-mr-charles-j-yellowplush: William Makepeace Thackeray's Memoirs of Mr. Charles J. Yellowplush show only a title page and contents here, so the tales themselves do not appear. The contents promise Miss Shum's Husband, then The Amours of Mr. Deuceace across chapters set partly in Paris. Yellowplush's farewell follows, along with Skimmings from the Dairy of George IV and Epistles to the Literati. The chapter headings keep the footman-narrator's comic misspellings, from 'Foring Parts' to 'Hitting the Nale on the Hedd.'
the-paris-sketch-book-of-mr-m-a-titmarsh:
William Makepeace Thackeray wrote The Paris Sketch Book under his pen name Mr. M. A. Titmarsh. The contents list sketches on an invasion of France, the Fêtes of July, the French school of painting, a gambler's death, Napoleon and his system, and caricatures and lithography in Paris. Four imitations of Béranger's songs are included, with versions in French and English.

The book opens with a dedicatory letter to M. Aretz, a Paris tailor of the Rue Richelieu. Thackeray tells him that every man should acknowledge and praise virtue wherever he finds it. The dedication sets a playful, personal tone for sketches of French life, art, drama, and politics by a young English observer.
the-present-state-of-wit-1711-and-excerp: John Gay's The Present State of Wit, dated 1711, is reprinted here as number 3 in a series of essays on wit from the Augustan Reprint Society, dated May 1947. Donald F. Bond supplies an introduction and a bibliographical note. Bound with it are excerpts from The English Theophrastus, or the Manners of the Age, from 1702, introduced by W. Earl Britton. The pages shown are the reprint's front matter, with the society's editors and advisors listed. The essays themselves are not shown.
the-strange-case-of-cavendish: Randall Parrish, author of When Wilderness Was King, published this mystery with the A. L. Burt Company in 1918, by arrangement with George H. Doran. Only the title pages and contents appear in this record. The contents list twenty-six chapters. They start with a decision and a body on the floor. Miss Donovan's arrival follows. A gang of enemies and a shot of death come next. Capture in the Shoshone desert follows. A cliff cave and Cavendish's reappearance close the list. The case itself does not appear.
the-tale-of-chloe-an-episode-in-the-hist:
George Meredith tells this episode in the history of Beau Beamish under an epigraph toasting fair Chloe, once queen of the festival meeting and now lifeless and cold. Chapter one begins with a proper tenderness for the peerage. An illustrious gentleman is inflamed by Cupid's darts. He would marry a dairymaid. Beamish named her the Duchess of Dewlap. He did so on her first day at the Wells.

Meredith explains the nickname's work. Beamish's happy name rescued a princely house from vulgar assault. The ballad of the Duke and the Dairymaid coloured the period's memory too. It was once popular enough to draw moralists' attacks. Writers of pretension, he complains, treat highwaymen gladly yet bestow only passing remarks on domestic kings like Beamish, the background against which Chloe's own story at the Wells will unfold.
the-way-of-all-flesh: Samuel Butler held this novel back until after his death in 1902: the story of Ernest Pontifex, who breaks free from a crushing Victorian father. Drawn from Butler's own youth, it is wry, brave, and quietly furious. The book that freed the English novel from the paterfamilias.
the-wept-of-wish-ton-wish:
J. Fenimore Cooper's Wept of Wish-Ton-Wish appears here in an 1871 printing, prefaced by a letter to a Pennsylvania clergyman who furnished the tale's materials. That correspondent's own descent, Cooper writes, runs back beyond recorded time, making him truly an American beside settlers of a brief century or two. The letter thanks him while respecting his wish to stay unnamed.

A preface follows on the difficulty of picturing early dangers vividly now. Indian traditions, Cooper says, are heard today with the interest lent to a dark age. Ancestors faced privations and perils while preparing a land now secure and abundant. The tale's humble object is to perpetuate recollection of some of those experiences before they fade entirely.
tish: Mary Roberts Rinehart published Tish, the chronicle of her escapades and excursions, in 1916, with illustrations by May Wilson Preston. Contents list five pieces: Mind over Motor, Like a Wolf on the Fold, The Simple Lifers, Tish's Spy, and a patriotic piece addressed to Tish herself. Illustration captions show Tish motoring home a winner, stalking into woods with a rabbit and knife, and canoeing toward Island Eleven. The front pages and captions are what is shown in this record, so Rinehart's stories themselves do not appear.
